stories.Headline: How Is NVIDIA Expanding AI-Powered Telecom Networks Following T-Mobile’s First AI-RAN Call?
stories.Summary:
T-Mobile, Nokia and Nvidia say they have completed the world's first AI-RAN voice call on a commercial mobile network. The call was made from a commercial cell site in Bellevue, Washington, where T-Mobile has its headquarters, and Nvidia announced it at its GTC Berlin event around October 21, 2026. It ran over T-Mobile's live production network using Nokia Massive MIMO radio and Nokia's 5G anyRAN software, on servers built around Nvidia's Aerial RAN Computer platform. The site was connected to a commercial 5G core and a commercially available smartphone, and Nokia says this shows AI-RAN moving out of controlled labs and onto live spectrum and commercial infrastructure.

The next phase of field trials will cover new AI-for-RAN algorithms, additional spectrum bands, and AI inferencing workloads running alongside radio functions on one shared accelerated computing platform. Nokia's first commercial AI-RAN products are not expected to go live until next year. Nokia's chief technology and AI officer, Pallavi Mahajan, said the company is on a path to doubling spectral efficiency, meaning more capacity from the same spectrum. Nvidia also unveiled two new configurations of its Aerial RAN Computer, called MGX 2U and MGX 4U, both using RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs with a choice of x86 or Nvidia Vera processors, and Dell Technologies, Quanta Cloud Technology and Supermicro are expected to offer servers for the platform.

Responsibility for the milestone sits with the three companies, with Nokia supplying the radio and software, Nvidia the computing platform and T-Mobile the live network and site. Mahajan described AI-RAN as an important evolution of the radio network, and said Nokia wants to turn the RAN into an increasingly software-defined, AI-native platform that can support future AI-enabled services and the move toward 6G. She added that each step of the trials brings the companies closer to understanding how AI-RAN can deliver real benefits and eventually operate at scale. Nvidia also said Nokia and Cisco are building its Nemotron AI models into their network management software, and that TCS, BT and NTT DATA are using them to develop AI agents for network management, site inspections and fault remediation.

The work builds on a 2024 agreement between Nokia and Nvidia to develop AI-ready RAN solutions, which came before Nvidia became an investor in Nokia, and on T-Mobile's announcement of an AI-RAN Innovation Center in Bellevue in September 2024. Several European operators are moving forward as well. BT plans live trials in Birmingham, England, during 2027, and Deutsche Telekom has validated the platform in labs in Bonn, Germany, and Oulu, Finland, with field trials planned for 2027. Elisa in Finland completed what Nokia and Nvidia call Europe's first AI-RAN field trial, running voice, mobile data and video analytics at once on a single platform. Nvidia says nine operators across Europe, the Middle East and Africa are building or expanding its infrastructure, but many projects remain at the lab or trial stage, and no financial terms or revenue expectations have been disclosed.

stories.Headline: Where What When - Un-Artificial Thoughts about Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Dr. Ephraim Horowitz published a two-part set of reflections on artificial intelligence in the Where What When print edition, with the first part appearing online in October 2026 and dated October 23, 2026. He opens by saying AI has gone from a nerdy science discipline a few years ago to one of the most influential driving forces of society. He notes the field has existed since 1956 and describes it as a branch of computer science aimed at getting computers to mimic human behavior. The print issue carries an ad deadline of Friday, November 13, 2026, and a publication date of Friday, November 20, 2026.

The piece argues, drawing on the Ramchal's Mesillas Yesharim, that technology is never neutral, since everything in the world can be used for good or for evil. As examples he cites nuclear energy, which supplies clean power, sterilizes food and has medical uses, but which also killed over 120,000 people within seconds at Hiroshima and Nagasaki. He also points to the printing press, invented in 1440, which spread information and Torah knowledge but also fed decadence. He then surveys image processing, robotics and large language models, noting the US Post Office began using automated handwriting recognition in 1950. On robots, he says car production time fell from about 30 hours in 1970 to 12 hours in 2026, and that over three million procedures were performed in 2025 with the da Vinci surgical system.

The author also lays out the darker side of these tools, using his own tests and figures from the sources he cites. He asked four chatbots to draw President Donald Trump chopping down a cherry tree: Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic Claude refused, while Grok produced an almost-real cartoon and Google Gemini produced a photo-quality likeness. He reports that Warren Buffett said AI-generated deepfake videos of himself are so convincing that even he might have been fooled into sending money. On drones, he writes that Ukraine produced over four million in 2025, which killed or wounded about 240,000 Russian troops and destroyed over 29,000 heavy weapon systems, while Sudan's drones targeted over 2,000 civilians in hundreds of attacks in the first quarter of 2026.

Horowitz also describes how large language models can mislead, recounting his search for a specific gemara in which Copilot gave him two wrong locations and then wrote out two lines of text. Only at the end did it admit that no such gemara existed and that it had fabricated what it showed him. He says this behavior is common enough to have a name, AI hallucination, and observes that chatbots once carried warnings that results might be inaccurate, though he has not seen them recently. The article's text breaks off while he is still discussing this point. The second article is labeled Part 1, which suggests more is to come, though the excerpts do not say when.

stories.Headline: Appeals court lifts block on Mississippi's DEI ban, ejects judge over AI errors
stories.Summary:
A federal appeals court on Thursday revived Mississippi's ban on diversity, equity and inclusion programs in public schools, wiping out a lower-court order that had kept the law from taking effect. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, based in New Orleans, ruled that the preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate could not stand. The three-judge panel also reassigned the lawsuit to a different district judge after finding that the original ruling was marred by errors tied to artificial intelligence. The case is Jackson Federation of Teachers et al. v. Lynn Fitch et al., number 25-60496.

The appeals court recognized the state's authority over curricula and said the law does not directly regulate students' speech. The law at issue is House Bill 1193, which the Mississippi Legislature enacted in 2025. It bars public schools and public postsecondary institutions from creating, promoting or implementing DEI programs, from maintaining offices that promote specified divisive concepts, from requiring or weighing diversity statements in hiring and admissions, and from compelling participation in DEI training. It also requires the State Department of Education, the Board of Trustees of State Institutions of Higher Learning and the Mississippi Community College Board to teach and promote the position that there are two genders, male and female, based on chromosomal makeup.

The attorney general and private parties can enforce the statute, and it calls for annual reporting. The lawsuit, filed June 9, 2025, was brought by teachers, professors, students and advocacy groups, who argued the law violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Wingate's first restraining order contained inaccuracies, including wrongly listed plaintiff names and mistakes about the bill's language. At oral argument, Circuit Judge Jerry Smith asked whether the court could be confident those errors had not affected the judge's ultimate reasoning.

In the ruling, the court wrote that the district court, or perhaps its AI agent if one wanted to be charitable, had ignored and manipulated governing law, apparently to satisfy a policy agenda. Wingate acknowledged in a letter that a law clerk used the AI tool Perplexity as a drafting assistant, and said the version docketed on July 20, 2025 was an early draft that had not gone through the court's standard review process. He sent the letter to Robert Conrad, director of the Administrative Office of the Courts, in response to an inquiry from Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley. Lawyers for Mississippi, including Anthony Shults of the attorney general's office, argued the errors undermined confidence in the court's legal reasoning and urged reassignment.

Plaintiffs' attorneys, led by Robert McDuff of the Mississippi Center for Justice, called the AI use a regrettable shortcut that did not affect the constitutionality question, and asked that the case stay with Wingate. The panel sided with the state. With the injunction vacated, the dispute returns to the district court under a new judge, and the constitutional questions the plaintiffs raised remain unresolved. Grassley's office has also flagged AI-related problems in orders from staff for a second federal judge, which the senator described as error-ridden.

stories.Headline: UAE's G42 signs pacts to explore AI infrastructure in Greece
stories.Summary:
Abu Dhabi's G42, a technology holding group, and five of its portfolio companies signed initial agreements with Greek government and private-sector partners on Friday, October 23, 2026, according to a company statement. The agreements cover AI infrastructure, government services, life sciences and smart cities. They were signed in Athens during an official visit by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, at the UAE-Greece Strategic Forum. G42 said the deals extend its Intelligence Grid, which spans data centres, advanced compute, cloud infrastructure and industry-specific applications, into Greece. G42's agreements were part of 18 memorandums of understanding, agreements and commercial partnerships between the UAE and Greece, valued at €12.75 billion, or $14.3 billion.

Under the deals with Greece's Copelouzos Group, Khazna Data Centres and Core42 will explore building an AI factory in the country. Khazna would lead development of the physical infrastructure, while Core42 would supply cloud and AI compute capabilities for organisations in banking, telecoms, shipping and government. Presight will work with Greece's Ministry of Digital Governance on urban mobility and municipal operations, starting with agentic AI for waste management and water-network monitoring using synthetic and open data. Two further agreements cover government services and health. Inception42 will work with the Greek ministry on using agentic AI in government and education, including tools to support cabinet meetings and track progress against government priorities, training for officials to work with AI agents, and AI tutors and learning platforms.

M42 signed a pact with Athens LifeTech Park covering life sciences research, genomics sequencing infrastructure, population genomics, clinical development and the linking of institutional biobanks. The research would focus on oncology, rare genetic diseases and neuroscience, and a bilateral programme would give UAE start-ups a base at the park's incubator for entering Europe, while Greek and European ventures gain access to the UAE through M42's network. Executives on both sides welcomed the agreements. Mansoor Al Mansoori, chief executive of G42 International, called them an important milestone in expanding the Intelligence Grid across Europe, and said the company would work with trusted local partners in line with European standards. Christos Copelouzos, chief executive of Copelouzos Group, said the AI factory would strengthen Greece's position as a digital and energy hub in South-east Europe, support the digital transformation of the economy, attract investment and create highly skilled jobs.

Greece's Minister of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence, Dimitris Papastergiou, said AI can make cities smarter, more efficient and safer, and that the focus is on practical uses that improve citizens' daily lives. Thomas Pramotedham of Presight said cities hold huge volumes of data whose value lies in turning it into intelligence, while Inception42's chief executive Ashish Koshy said each programme would follow European standards for responsible AI. The agreements are initial and exploratory, and the articles give no timeline for the next steps. G42 has been helping countries build domestic AI capabilities, and in February it signed a framework agreement with a Vietnamese consortium to develop sovereign AI capabilities and cloud infrastructure in that country.

stories.Headline: OpenAI cuts valuation target by $150 bn to $1.25 tn | Why it has scaled back its funding ambitions ahead of IPO
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has lowered the valuation it is seeking from new investors by $150 billion, to $1.25 trillion, according to reports published on October 22 and 23, 2026. The company had discussed a figure of $1.4 trillion earlier in the talks, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg. The cut reportedly followed resistance from some investors, though no reason for the lower figure was reported, and OpenAI declined to comment. Both numbers are pre-money prices, so they exclude the new capital being raised, and the discussions are ongoing, which means the final terms could still change.

The talks concern a funding round of up to $30 billion, with Coatue Management in talks to co-lead and investment funds from the United Arab Emirates, along with firms including BlackRock, also involved. Nothing has been signed, but OpenAI expects investor commitments to be finalised by the end of next week, and the final size of the round is still under discussion. OpenAI is also negotiating a separate deal to buy more computing capacity from the UAE. At $1.25 trillion, OpenAI would be the most valuable private company ever, and well above the $852 billion valuation it received in March, when it raised $122 billion from investors including Amazon, SoftBank and NVIDIA.

The revision comes as technology stocks fell this week after mixed quarterly results from companies including Meta Platforms and Tesla, which added to investor scrutiny of how much is being spent on artificial intelligence. On Thursday the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.60% to 26,008.86, its steepest fall since early June. Microsoft, OpenAI's largest listed backer, fell 2.23% to $521.08 that day, then edged up 0.18% in after-hours trading. Microsoft valued its stake in OpenAI at about $135 billion after the October 2025 restructuring, roughly 27 percent on an as-converted diluted basis, though the March round has likely diluted that share and no updated figure has been disclosed. Microsoft reports fiscal first-quarter results on October 28.

On the question of going public, OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the US Securities and Exchange Commission in June but has not disclosed a listing date. Chief financial officer Sarah Friar told employees in August that the company "will be a public company in 2027," while chief executive Sam Altman said the following month that listing at that point would be "an ill-advised moment." The IPO has been pushed back to next year, with the company citing its focus on AI safety efforts. Rival Anthropic is preparing an IPO expected next month, reportedly seeking a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion after raising $65 billion in May at a $965 billion valuation, and OpenAI reportedly wants its commitments in place before Anthropic's filings make the two easier to compare. Separately, Chinese AI startup DeepSeek has raised about 100 billion yuan, or $14.98 billion, from investors including GigaDevice, Meituan and Geely, doubling its original target of 50 billion yuan.

stories.Headline: Federal privacy legislation in 2026: The 49 bills reshaping US data privacy law
stories.Summary:
The United States still has no single comprehensive federal privacy law like Europe's GDPR, but Congress has been busy. By September 2026, lawmakers in the 119th Congress had introduced a large collection of proposals covering consumer privacy, artificial intelligence, children's data, employee surveillance, reproductive information, precise location data, financial information, connected vehicles, data brokers, automated decision-making and age verification. The IAPP's September 2026 tracker counts 49 distinct proposals across five broad privacy categories, and several have House and Senate companions, so the number of bill numbers is higher. Only two of the tracked proposals have become law: the TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed May 19, 2025, and the Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act, signed September 5, 2025.

Three competing comprehensive consumer privacy bills are now under debate. The Online Privacy Act of 2026, introduced March 19, 2026, and referred to three House committees, would create rights of access, correction, deletion and portability, add data minimization and security requirements, protect people from automated decisions, and set up a new Digital Privacy Agency. Sen. Jerry Moran's Consumer Data Privacy and Security Act, introduced March 25 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, would set nationwide rights, impose security and accountability duties, and override covered state laws, with no private right of action. H.R. 8413, the SECURE Data Act, would regulate controllers, processors and data brokers, cover sensitive information and opt-outs, preempt covered state rules, and lack a general private right of action; it remained at committee stage in the latest official material reviewed.

The articles, which come from Stacker and were written with analysis from Captain Compliance, say the central fights are over state-law preemption and private lawsuits. Industry groups such as the Software & Information Industry Association back national uniformity, arguing companies need one framework instead of a growing patchwork. California regulators and a coalition of attorneys general argue that SECURE would wipe out stronger protections already in state law. Many other bills in the tracker either preserve state laws, preempt them, or say nothing, and a long list of proposals, including the Online Privacy Act, the Stop Spying Bosses Act and the My Body, My Data Act, would let individuals sue directly. Other measures include the Auto Data Privacy and Autonomy Act, which would limit carmakers' use and sharing of vehicle data without owner consent, and the Data Care Act, which would impose duties of care, loyalty and confidentiality on online service providers.

For context, the Future of Privacy Forum counted 21 comprehensive state privacy laws when the SECURE Data Act was introduced in April 2026. Almost 40% of the tracked proposals concern children or education, and AI provisions appear across consumer, worker and children's bills. Ideas once found mainly in comprehensive bills, such as data minimization, deletion rights, opt-outs and limits on targeted advertising, are showing up in narrower sector bills. The articles say that whether a federal law ends the need for fifty-state analysis depends on which model survives, and they do not describe a scheduled next step beyond the committee referrals noted above.

stories.Headline: Microsoft says China-linked hackers used AI penetration testing tool ARTEX to compromise ConnectWise as part of a campaign targeting hundreds of organizations (AJ Vicens/Reuters)
stories.Summary:
Microsoft said on Wednesday that a China state-aligned group it tracks as Storm-0940 was behind the recent supply chain compromise of the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application. According to Microsoft, the group used ARTEX, a Go-based agentic AI penetration testing framework, to speed up scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying, and abuse of OAuth applications at downstream victims. ARTEX was made closed-source after it was abused in attacks on South Korean financial institutions. Microsoft said the AI tool let the attackers work at machine speed against hundreds of organizations worldwide since September 2026.

The reported figures show how fast the campaign moved. Between October 10 and 14, 2026, infrastructure at 144.172.64[.]99 ran an automated cross-tenant password-spray campaign against 327 accounts across eight organizations, aiming at Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online. Microsoft captured more than 151,000 failed logon events in that window, peaking on October 11 at 2,900 failures per minute and more than 111,000 failures in a single day. Forty-eight accounts each received over 1,000 failures, but Microsoft detected no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call, or directory change at that stage. In the ConnectWise case, Storm-0940 was also seen using ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 attempts per minute, a pace Microsoft said leaves defenders little time to detect and respond.

The picture changed on October 15, 2026, when the AI agents gained access to the identities of several ConnectWise cloud applications and used them to authenticate into customer environments. Microsoft said this let the group operate without an interactive user sign-in, because the applications had already been granted access. The follow-on activity included reconnaissance, changes to application credentials, and attempts to alter privileges that could allow wider or lasting access. In a number of cases the attackers obtained privileged access to an organization's cloud infrastructure, and in several of them less than 3 hours passed between initial targeting and privileged access. Targeted sectors included aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits.

Microsoft attributed the activity to Storm-0940, a group it first described in November 2024. At that time it said the actor used a botnet called Quad7, also known as CovertNetwork-1658, to run highly evasive password spray attacks, and it assesses the group to have been active since at least 2021. The group is also known to exploit internet-facing applications for initial access and then use compromised accounts to move through target networks. It has also been seen adding credentials to existing OAuth applications in cloud environments to keep access to Microsoft 365 resources. The articles do not say what steps ConnectWise or affected organizations will take next.

stories.Headline: Sources: Anthropic and London-based PE firm Hg agree to launch a consultancy by the end of 2026 to embed AI consultants and engineers into European businesses (Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic and the London-based private equity firm Hg have agreed to set up an independent company that will place consultants and engineers inside European businesses to help them put artificial intelligence to work, according to a Financial Times report published on October 23, 2026. The report relied on unnamed sources, and the news was picked up by Techmeme and PYMNTS. The consultancy is expected to launch by the end of 2026. Neither Anthropic nor Hg had immediately responded to a request for comment from PYMNTS.

On the details, the articles say the new company will have hubs in London and Berlin and will be run as an independent business rather than as a unit of either partner. Its job is to embed AI consultants and engineers directly into the client firms it serves. The articles do not give a funding figure, ownership split, staffing numbers or a named leader. They also do not say which companies will be its first clients.

The two sides already have a track record together. Hg said in September that it was extending its existing collaboration with Anthropic to bring agentic AI capabilities to the companies in its portfolio. The firms had been working together for three years, on efforts that include a joint AI hackathon series and staff enablement inside Hg itself. Hg's co-CEOs, Steve Batchelor and JB Brian, said in that September release that Hg backed agentic AI early, that the relationship with Anthropic is central to this, and that they want portfolio companies to have a direct line to the frontier of the technology.

The move fits a wider pattern of demand for hands-on AI implementation. A report in May said monthly job listings for forward-deployed engineers rose by more than 800% between January and September 2025, a sign of how quickly companies are creating roles focused on putting AI systems to work inside enterprises. In May, Anthropic also teamed up with Goldman Sachs, Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman on a venture that helps large companies build its Claude model into their operations. Anthropic's chief financial officer, Krishna Rao, said at the time that partnerships with leading systems integrators are central to how Claude reaches big enterprises, and that the new firm would add operating capability and capital from alternative asset managers. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned launch by year end.

stories.Headline: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia had record lobbying quarters
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, Anthropic and OpenAI each posted their highest-spending lobbying quarter between July and September, according to federal disclosures reported by Lauren Feiner of The Verge on October 22, 2026. Nvidia spent the most at $2.2 million, followed by Anthropic at $2.1 million and OpenAI at $1.5 million, nearly $6 million combined. Apple also had a record quarter, spending $3.1 million, the first time it has reported more than $3 million on lobbying. The report treats the figures as a sign that the AI firms see shaping policy as increasingly important.

The disclosures show a spread of topics. Anthropic listed bills and orders it raised with Congress and the White House, including AI-related provisions in the Kids Online Safety Act, export control provisions in the AI Overwatch Act, Trump's executive order renaming AI "Super Intelligence," and the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would put data center energy costs on their developers. OpenAI lobbied Congress, the White House, the Small Business Administration and the Commerce and State Departments on cybersecurity evaluations for frontier models, AI safety oversight frameworks and antitrust protections for information sharing, along with copyright. Nvidia lobbied Congress, several agencies and White House offices on 6G networks, "responsible AI design," competition policy, quantum computing and export controls. Apple engaged on intellectual property, tariffs, kids online safety, competition and domestic chip manufacturing, including bills that would make app stores verify users' ages.

The companies are the ones responsible for the spending, but the disclosures list only high-level topics and the companies' own comments are not given in the reporting. The Verge reads OpenAI's lobbying as looking like a response to some of the fallout from the Hugging Face attack, though the filings do not say so directly. The article also notes that tech CEOs were already visible in Washington, with many attending a White House lunch with President Donald Trump in late September that produced a "morally binding" AI safety accord. The filings suggest more discussions were happening behind the scenes, just before Trump named his AI czar and task force.

The sums are not unusual next to long-established Washington players, since Microsoft has spent at least $2 million a quarter since 2021 and Google regularly spends over $3 million. What stands out is how quickly the AI firms have ramped up. OpenAI did not spend even $1 million in a single quarter until this year, and did not top half a million until the end of 2024, while Anthropic's biggest quarter last year was just over $1 million. This was also the first quarter in which Nvidia spent more than $2 million. With Democrats expected to win back at least some control of Congress in the midterm elections, and some lawmakers viewing a crackdown on the industry as a winning issue, the report expects lobbying to keep rising whichever party holds power next year.

stories.Headline: Websites go dark worldwide as AI uncovers flaws in code powering much of the internet
stories.Summary:
Governments and companies around the world took websites offline on Oct 22 as they rushed to guard against hacks, after artificial intelligence uncovered two critical flaws in PHP, a programming language that helps run about 70% of the world's websites, according to Wiz Research. The PHP Foundation, which maintains the language, released emergency security updates on Oct 21 for the two flaws, which are known collectively as PHP2Shell. The security firm Calif found the first flaw on Aug 1 using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, during an OpenAI-funded audit of the language's code. Wiz, which is owned by Google, found its own flaw independently on Aug 19, using Google's Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-5.6 Sol and its own research agent. Details leaked online on Oct 20, a day before the planned fix, which set off the scramble to pull sites offline before hackers could act.

The flaws can let attackers into servers without a username or password, and both carry a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10. The US National Security Agency told organisations to patch immediately or take vulnerable systems offline, and authorities from Japan to the European Union said the same. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged updates to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, and the FBI advised organisations to list every place PHP runs, including products that bundle it. Government sites in Australia, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Denmark went dark, while in Japan MUFG Bank halted some online transactions, Mizuho stopped services, Shizuoka Bank shut its banking app, and All Nippon Airways disabled boarding passes in Apple Wallet. The network that settles funds between almost all Japanese banks was not affected.

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore said the flaws affect all versions of PHP and reported widespread exploitation attempts and several proof-of-concept exploits, though it knew of no Singapore sites taken down by hackers. The Government Technology Agency of Singapore said there was currently no sign any government systems had been compromised, and that some services might be taken offline temporarily as a precaution. The PHP Foundation said anyone running PHP must update now, and one of its security engineers, Volker Dusch, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem the language has faced in over a decade, comparable to the Heartbleed flaw of 2014. A Wiz blog post said the findings rank among the most severe ever found in PHP, and arguably in software history. OpenAI said the discovery marks a new phase in which AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact, and it also warned that such tools can help attackers build exploits.

Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed, and many large platforms use other languages or operators able to install the fix quickly, so they stayed online. Cybersecurity lecturer Rahat Masood of the University of New South Wales called the discovery quite devastating, saying attackers who get in can do almost anything, from stealing information to changing site content. Steve Kerrison of James Cook University's Singapore campus said larger institutions should patch quickly, but many smaller sites and user-run blogs may stay vulnerable for days, weeks or months and could be used to spread viruses or spam. So far there is little evidence of damaging attacks, though data breaches could later feed phishing campaigns. The number of software vulnerabilities found worldwide in 2026 is on track to roughly double the record total set in 2025, and Cloudflare has reported millions of exploit attempts since the disclosure.

stories.Headline: LG Electronics to Bring Robots, AI to World's Largest Tidal Power Plant
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics signed a memorandum of understanding with Korea Water Resources Corporation, known as K-water, on Oct. 22 at the Sihwa Tidal Culture Center in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province. The agreement covers the Sihwa Lake tidal power plant, which has the largest generation capacity of any tidal plant in the world. The two sides agreed to turn the facility into an AI-powered smart plant, applying digital twins and robots on site. They also agreed to cooperate on research and development, policy and expansion abroad.

The company will first use digital twin technology to copy the whole plant in a virtual space and link it to real-time data from generation equipment and closed-circuit cameras. That setup is meant to allow forecasts of power output, testing of operating scenarios and diagnosis of equipment conditions. LG is also considering an AI agent built on Exaone, the proprietary model from LG AI Research, to analyze output losses, spot equipment faults, support predictive maintenance, assess risks and tune inspection schedules. For work on site, patrol robots, AI-equipped cameras and industrial robots would handle facility patrols, equipment inspections, monitoring of hazardous areas, and the storage and transport of spare parts.

Lee Seung-ki, head of LG Electronics' Smart Factory Solution Center, said it is significant that skills built on manufacturing floors are now being applied to public infrastructure. He said the company will work with K-water to support the plant's digital transformation and keep improving its operating efficiency and safety. The Korea Times reported the company's statement in similar terms. LG framed the project as a reference case for taking its smart factory solutions into energy infrastructure at home and overseas.

The deal marks the first time LG has carried smart factory technology from manufacturing into public infrastructure such as power plants, according to The Elec. The company wants to grow beyond its existing manufacturing and logistics clients and join energy projects led by governments and large corporations. Cumulative orders for its smart factory solutions business passed 1 trillion won in the first half of 2026, two years after the unit's launch. The articles describe the digital twin, AI agent and robotics work as items to be examined or tested, and they give no timeline or cost for the upgrades.

stories.Headline: India's Tech Mahindra partners with SpaceXSI for AI-powered software development - CNA
stories.Summary:
Tech Mahindra, the Indian IT services company, announced on Thursday, October 22, that it has partnered with SpaceXSI to use artificial intelligence to modernise legacy applications and speed up software development. Reuters-style coverage described Tech Mahindra as India's fifth-largest IT firm. The company will also bring in the chatbot Grok Build to set up industry-specific solutions. The announcement did not say when the joint offering will become available.

The deal combines Tech Mahindra's engineering and enterprise transformation services with SpaceXSI's development platform. The two sides plan to concentrate on software delivery, code quality and developer productivity across technology, telecommunications, banking and financial services, manufacturing, healthcare and retail. They also intend to run joint go-to-market initiatives, customer engagements and industry-specific programmes. Tech Mahindra will set up enablement and certification programmes to help client engineering teams adopt the tools.

Toni Adams, Head of Global Partnerships at SpaceXSI, said in the announcement that most enterprises already accept that AI will change how software is built. What they lack, she said, is expertise in rolling it out across large and varied engineering teams without breaking what already works. Tech Mahindra said it will fold Grok Build expertise into its engineering transformation and application modernisation services. The companies described the offering as designed for enterprise settings, where governance, security and compliance are requirements.

Tech Mahindra already has similar pacts with Google Gemini and Microsoft, but this is the first time an Indian IT major has teamed up with the AI division of rocket maker SpaceX. The company did not name any customer deployments, disclose financial terms or put a figure on expected productivity gains. It has also not said how much revenue, if any, it expects the collaboration to bring in. Separately, Tech Mahindra plans to report its AI revenue on its own starting in the second half of fiscal 2027.

stories.Headline: SK Hyper Seeks $350 Billion for First 5GW Phase of 15GW AI Data Center Plan
stories.Summary:
SK Hyper, the AI data center arm of SK Telecom, said it is seeking about $350 billion, or 463 trillion won, to fund the first 5-gigawatt phase of a plan to build 15 gigawatts of data center capacity in South Korea. Chief executive Chung Suk-keun laid out the strategy on October 23 during an appearance on Bloomberg TV's "Bloomberg Tech: Asia." The goal is to draw global companies' AI infrastructure into the country and capture computing demand from elsewhere in Asia, including Japan and Taiwan. The company hopes this will turn South Korea into a global AI infrastructure hub.

The plan calls for 15GW of capacity by 2035, with phased operations starting in 2029 to reach the initial 5GW. The $350 billion estimate for that first phase includes servers and other equipment. SK Hyper intends to build a cluster of more than 2GW in the Yeongnam region, beginning with its AI data center in Ulsan, and to add gigawatt-scale facilities in the Chungcheong and southwestern regions. It aims to land its first outside investment late this year or early next year, then raise more money over the following three to four years, sharing the total cost with data center customers and outside investors. SK Telecom has previously said it would invest up to 750 billion won in SK Hyper in stages through 2030.

Chung said he does not expect much difficulty securing power and sites for the first 5GW, and that the biggest challenges will be securing real demand in the global market and raising the capital needed. He explained that South Korea's data center market is currently about 1GW, which has made the country unattractive in the global industry until now, and that the initial 5GW is roughly five times that figure. For this reason, SK Hyper is talking with global hyperscalers about bringing AI inference hubs to Korea and wants to attract training computing infrastructure as well. According to Bloomberg, Chung said revenue could begin as early as next year, ahead of 2029, when the first data centers are scheduled for completion.

Chung argued that actual computing demand remains firm despite a recent pullback in AI infrastructure stocks and weaker investor sentiment, saying AI model developers and service providers see customer demand rising sharply. He said the company should prepare in advance rather than wait for demand to appear, while managing risk by confirming demand with big tech firms and hyperscalers before investing. He also said the competitive edge has shifted from who holds the most graphics processing units to who can generate tokens at the lowest cost with the highest efficiency. SK Hyper plans to combine SK Group's semiconductor, energy and telecommunications strengths, and Chung added that many countries want sovereign AI infrastructure they can control at home, a trend he expects to spread. Expansion from 5GW to 15GW will depend on global customer demand.

stories.Headline: Sri Lanka launches UNESCO’s AI Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM)
stories.Summary:
UNESCO's Regional Office for South Asia, working with Sri Lanka's Ministry of Digital Economy, has launched the organisation's Readiness Assessment Methodology, known as RAM, for artificial intelligence in the country. A National Steering Committee held its first meeting in Colombo on 20 May 2026 and a second on 2 September 2026, and UNESCO announced the launch on 22 October 2026. RAM is a tool for helping countries put UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence into practice, by assessing whether a nation is ready to develop and use AI in a responsible, ethical and inclusive way. Sri Lanka is among the first few countries to run the exercise with RAM 2.0, an updated version of the original method.

The assessment will produce a report meant to complement Sri Lanka's digital transformation agenda and its proposed national AI strategy. Based on the country's strengths, gaps and priorities, it will offer practical recommendations for building a human-centred AI ecosystem in line with international standards and ethical innovation. Several multi-stakeholder consultations are planned over the coming months in Colombo, Jaffna, Kandy, Batticaloa and Galle. LIRNEasia, a Colombo-based economic and digital policy think tank, has been brought in as the national implementation partner.

The Steering Committee is chaired by Waruna Sri Dhanapala, Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Economy, and Eunsong Kim, Chief of Social and Human Sciences at the UNESCO Regional Office for South Asia. Its members include other government agencies, the Sri Lanka National Commission for UNESCO, private sector leaders, academics, civil society experts and Citra Lab at the United Nations Development Programme. Its main job is to guide the assessment and make sure it captures the complexity of Sri Lanka's AI ecosystem across every dimension and policy area RAM covers. At the meetings, participants noted that AI and its ethical use are a priority for the government, and stressed that policymaking should be inclusive and draw on voices from across society.

The launch sits alongside other AI efforts in Sri Lanka. As of August 2026, UNESCO has used RAM in more than 75 Member States, with the process finished in 60, including India, Bangladesh and the Maldives in South Asia. Separately, Biometric Update reported on 23 October that Sri Lanka is seeking Chinese support for a National Sovereign AI Computing Centre. The country has about 5 megawatts of data center capacity, while officials estimate it needs between 25 and 50 megawatts of cloud and AI computing capacity in the short term. Deputy Minister of Digital Economy Eranga Weeraratne and Chinese Ambassador Wei Huaxiang discussed cooperation, and the two countries are working toward a memorandum of understanding on AI.

stories.Headline: Harvard College students are using newly expanded access to Anthropic’s Claude for coursework, extracurricular projects, and personal tasks after the Faculty of Arts and Sciences began providing institutional access to the AI platform this summer. The FAS fir
stories.Summary:
Harvard College students are using newly widened access to Anthropic's Claude for coursework, extracurricular projects and personal tasks, according to the Harvard Crimson. The Faculty of Arts and Sciences began providing institutional access to the AI platform this summer. The change was first announced in April, when the FAS said it would add Claude to its suite of available AI tools while moving ChatGPT Edu to a request-only basis. The handover of tool availability to Harvard affiliates took place over the summer, and students are now in their first semester with the FAS-sponsored access.

Students described a wide range of uses. In General Education 1201, on neuroscience and artificial intelligence, Claude is built into the syllabus and assignments, which Iris A. Heikkinen '29 said teaches students how to use AI for studying. Leonardo Miranda '30 is using it in a first-year seminar called "Letting Claude Cook," where students must use the tool for a class project, and he said there is no cap on how many credits a student can use. Santiago D. Revilla '30 built a website that pulls in his Google Calendar and shows the weather for each day so he can plan walks and runs, while Ankit Biswas '30, a research fellow at the Cambridge Boston Align Initiative, uses Claude to scaffold ideas and handle implementation. Sean "Brady" Merrill '30 said he has used Claude Premium to help build models for a racing boat club he belongs to.

Responsibility for the rollout rests with the FAS, which made the April announcement and oversaw the summer transition. The seminar Miranda described is taught by Douglas P. Finkbeiner, the FAS's senior adviser on generative AI, who previously worked for Anthropic. Some students tied their preference for Claude to their views of the company. Merrill said he favors it because Anthropic's leadership and staff did not sign a deal with the Pentagon, a reference to a dispute earlier this year between Anthropic and the Department of Defense over AI safety safeguards. Conner M. Lewandowski '30 said he would rather support a company whose vision for AI and moral outlook match his own.

The Harvard access sits alongside a broader push by Anthropic into academia, including a new Guest Investigators program reported by Tech Times. The company opened a call on Wednesday for principal investigators at academic institutions, nonprofits and government labs to apply for embedded research collaborations lasting 8 to 12 weeks, with extensions possible for some projects. The program covers five life sciences areas, including causal human biology, drug discovery and clinical science, and excludes private companies and startups. Anthropic pays all model-compute costs, and researchers keep their data and the right to pursue follow-on work, while Anthropic commits to open-sourcing accompanying code and data and to publishing results jointly. The application window runs about 14 days from October 22, 2026, and Anthropic has said it will try to notify selected participants roughly 14 days after applications close.

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s AI diagnostic tool outperforms general physicians in complex cases, study finds
stories.Summary:
Microsoft researchers have reported that an AI system they built diagnosed complex medical cases more accurately than practicing generalist physicians, according to a study published October 22, 2026 in Science. The system, called the Diagnostic Orchestrator, or DxO, runs on a commercial large language model, GPT-5 in the main results, and simulates a panel of physicians who track a differential diagnosis, challenge leading hypotheses and weigh the cost of each test. On 304 New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases it reached the correct diagnosis 83.2% of the time, versus 36.1% for generalist physicians who could use search and reference tools. On 325 emergency department admissions drawn from the MIMIC-IV-ED database, it scored 80.3%, against 46.8% for physicians.

The study built a benchmark called SDBench, in which each case begins with a brief clinical vignette and the diagnostician must decide what history to take, which tests to order and when to commit to a diagnosis. A separate AI gatekeeper released information only when asked, and test costs were estimated from hospital chargemaster pricing. Physicians averaged 22.3% accuracy without reference tools, and the best individual physician reached 51.8% on the conference cases and 62.5% on the emergency cases. Physicians asked 5.6 questions on average before ordering a first test, while DxO asked 25.5. Without budget limits, DxO's testing cost more than the physicians' ($5,431 versus $4,725 on the conference cases, $4,979 versus $3,400 on the emergency cases), but budget-limited versions scored 80.9% at $2,241 and 79.6% at $1,303 on the conference cases, and 73.2% at $2,634 and 69.5% at $2,037 on the emergency cases.

All 15 authors are Microsoft employees, including Microsoft AI chief executive Mustafa Suleyman, Dominic King and Eric Horvitz, and they hold equity in the company, which sells AI and health care services. Eight authors are named inventors on a Microsoft patent application tied to the evaluation framework, and the study had no outside funding. The authors argue that static benchmarks, which hand over a full case write-up at once, can overstate AI ability because they cannot show whether a system asks the right questions, avoids needless testing or knows when to stop. They suggested the AI's edge may come from its breadth of knowledge and its consistency, without fatigue, time pressure or cognitive bias.

The authors acknowledged limits. The comparison was against individual generalists, not specialists or teams, and they expect the gap to narrow against specialists matched to each case. The NEJM cases are chosen for teaching value, the benchmark was text-only with no imaging or pathology slides, and every case had a pathological diagnosis, so healthy and benign visits were left out. Cost estimates used standardized U.S. pricing, and the study did not assess treatment, patient safety or outcomes. Next, the authors plan to design workflows in which clinicians and AI work together, and see potential uses in medical education and continuing professional development.

stories.Headline: Kansas City lab to train AI to predict protein changes tied to ALS, Alzheimer’s
stories.Summary:
A Kansas City research lab has been chosen to take part in a $28.6 million national effort to train artificial intelligence to predict protein changes linked to neurodegenerative disease. KCTV reported the news on October 21, 2026. Investigator Randal Halfmann and a team of local scientists at the Stowers Institute for Medical Research received a $4.1 million grant as their share of the project. They will use technology in new ways to help predict harmful protein changes tied to Alzheimer's, Huntington's and ALS.

Halfmann's lab will produce more than 10 billion measurements covering 50,000 proteins and over a million samples. This data is meant to teach AI to recognize the moment when something begins to go wrong. The task is hard because AI can readily detect many proteins but struggles with those involved in diseases such as Alzheimer's, which keep changing shape. The microscopic protein clumping under study will be collected at a level of detail never achieved before.

Halfmann said the question behind the work has motivated biology for roughly 60 years. He believes the effort will lay groundwork for generations, and his ultimate aim is to predict when a person will develop a disease and how quickly it will progress. He expects the data to create a much larger pool of people entering clinical trials, which would give those trials the power to find therapies that work. He also said he is optimistic that in two years researchers will be in a much better position to act.

His team has been working on this problem for years, and in 2023 the Stowers lab first identified the molecular trigger behind toxic protein buildup in Huntington's disease. With millions of Americans affected by neurodegenerative disease, Halfmann said the situation creates a sense of urgency, and he does not take any day for granted because every day matters to patients. The $28.6 million effort brings together select scientists from a handful of top institutions and universities around the country. KCTV pointed readers to the project's website for more on this and other research.

stories.Headline: Micron Technology Maps AI Memory Future With HBM, DRAM and NAND Roadmap
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology laid out a roadmap for AI-focused memory and storage during its technology and product leadership webinar, which was reported on October 21, 2026. Scott DeBoer, the company's president and chief technology and products officer, said AI is turning memory from a supporting part into a central limit on system performance, capacity and cost per token. He said Micron wants to advance memory, storage and compute together, with higher bandwidth, larger capacities, better power efficiency and closer work with customers. The presentation covered next-generation DRAM, high-bandwidth memory, NAND and advanced packaging.

On DRAM, DeBoer said the 1-gamma node is already in high-volume manufacturing and will underpin products introduced over the coming 12 months. The 1-delta node is expected to enter volume production in the second half of 2027, aiming for a mid-20% percentage gain in bit density and tuned for AI products such as HBM5, vertical HBM and vertical edge inference memory. Micron is also working on 1-epsilon, 1-zeta and eta-generation technologies, using wafer bonding, High-NA EUV and new materials. Beyond that, LPDDR6 is expected to offer 35% better power performance than LPDDR5, DDR6 is being developed with customers at twice the bandwidth of DDR5, and a 1-terabyte RDIMM is planned after the recently sampled 512-gigabyte DDR5 RDIMM.

For high-bandwidth memory, Micron said it is in high-volume manufacturing with HBM4 and is developing both standard and customized versions, with custom designs placing customer-specific memory and logic technology in the base die. It also described vertical HBM, which would put memory directly on top of processors to deliver much greater bandwidth, though capacity will grow more slowly because of heat challenges. Hybrid bonding will matter more as interconnect pitches shrink, and the company is working on taller stacks and thermal tools such as heat spreaders over the hotter parts of the base die. Future base dies will use foundry nodes, and HBM4E will need more advanced CMOS to meet speed and power goals, although HBM4 did not. In NAND, Generation 11 is set to ramp in the second half of 2027, with more than double the bit density of Generation 9, a target of 1.5 times the I/O speed, lower data-transfer energy, wafer-on-wafer bonding and more than 400 layers.

DeBoer was the main voice, and in the question session he rejected the idea that 4F² DRAM designs inherently beat 6F² designs on density, saying capacitor pitch is what fundamentally sets bit density. He said scaling 4F² further runs into basic physics problems that will eventually bring in 3D DRAM instead, though timing will depend on cost, complexity and device performance. He said memory setups will differ across training, inference, edge and rack-scale systems, but more memory and bandwidth will keep improving performance. He added that Micron does not expect memory supply to come into balance over the next two years, citing earlier comments from company leadership.

Micron said it is also using AI internally, citing a data center controller that went from silicon to tape-out in half the time of the prior generation and a data center SSD developed with 60% less time than the one before. Longer-term investments include expanded Micron Ventures activity, work at Albany NanoTech on advanced lithography and a previously announced $10 billion, 10-year commitment to Micron Research Labs. The company is collaborating with partners from startup Liqid to Meta, and it recently published a white paper with Meta on optimizing LPDDR6 for data centers. The articles do not describe further scheduled events beyond the 2027 production dates.

stories.Headline: Asia's AI data center boom faces 'reality check' from public markets
stories.Summary:
Data center companies across Asia are coming under closer investor scrutiny after a run of stalled initial public offerings and bumpy stock market debuts, according to Nikkei Asia in a report dated October 23, 2026. The article says these setbacks, seen in Australia and South Korea, have raised questions about how richly the booming infrastructure business is valued. Providers such as Singapore's DayOne and Australia's NextDC are described as suffering as investors grow more skeptical of the AI infrastructure buildout. Related headlines listed alongside the piece point to specific damage, including a 40 percent share fall at NextDC after a backlash over power use.

Those headlines also say the Nvidia-backed provider Firmus scrapped a $5 billion Australian IPO, and that SK Hynix abandoned a plan to float its US unit, citing market volatility. A further item notes that Nvidia is to provide up to $105 billion in guarantees for OpenAI's Ohio data center. The Nikkei piece is credited to Tsubasa Suruga and Shaun Turton, filing from Tokyo and Canberra. The excerpt available gives no valuation figures or investor statements beyond this general picture of growing concern.

A column by Oxford professor Ian Goldin, published by the Korea Times on October 21, argues that the same boom carries economic risks. He writes that about $2.4 trillion is being spent on the AI buildout, fueled by rising debt and inflated private-equity and stock-market valuations. In his view, the bubble will burst at some point, and the resulting crash would hit retirement savings and consumer confidence, slow growth and could trigger a recession. He adds that data centers' electricity demands could push up energy costs, keeping inflation and interest rates higher than they would otherwise be.

Goldin also describes a growing public revolt against data centers, which he says are blamed for higher energy prices, make noise, use large amounts of water and offer few long-term local jobs. He criticizes forecasts from figures such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei, who predicted US growth rising from 2 percent to 10 to 15 percent, and Elon Musk, who expects growth to more than double to above 4 percent next year. A Korea JoongAng Daily opinion item from October 22 adds that, as demand for high-bandwidth memory surges, the key measure for investors may become the total cost of completing AI tasks rather than memory volume alone. The available excerpts do not say what happens next for the stalled listings.

stories.Headline: Why AI data centers are powering a boom in fuel-cell demand
stories.Summary:
On September 30, Hitachi, Brookfield Japan, Hartree Partners Singapore and Tokyo Gas signed a memorandum of understanding to work together on green data centers in Japan, and the companies announced it on October 23, 2026. The agreement builds on an earlier one among Hitachi, Brookfield and Hartree that was announced in July 2025, with Tokyo Gas now added as a fourth party. The companies want to design data centers that generate their own power, use it reliably and efficiently, and help cut emissions through green energy and related measures. As their first projects, they plan to build green data centers in the Kanto and Kyushu regions.

The four companies will draw up a basic concept for these power-integrated facilities and push toward a standardized model that can be rolled out flexibly. The design has four parts. First, on-site generation would be the main power source, combined with battery storage, grid power and other sources. Second, redundancy would be built into the whole infrastructure, including cooling and power distribution, so operations continue through equipment failures or swings in supply. Third, the group will set decarbonization requirements, covering carbon credits, environmental attributes and renewable energy, and fourth, major facilities such as buildings and on-site power plants would be standardized and modularized to shorten project lead times and allow scalable deployment.

The companies say the approach should reduce heavy reliance on the power grid, widen the choice of sites, encourage local production and consumption of energy, and speed up projects. They describe the effort as a way to combine their respective expertise to tackle securing power, keeping operations stable and decarbonizing AI data centers. Their release points to Japan's surge in data center construction, especially in urban areas, which is raising electricity demand and stretching the time needed to secure power capacity because of grid limits. It also notes that the Japanese government, as part of its Green Transformation initiatives, has promoted sustainable infrastructure and spreading data centers across regions.

The same pressure is visible in the United States, where data centers took 4.4% of electricity use in 2024, according to the Department of Energy. Penn State's Institute of Energy and the Environment says consumption could triple by 2028, and a Bloomberg analysis projects data centers could use as much as 20% of US electricity production by 2035. Andrew Denis of the energy technology firm ZON said roughly half of the data center projects due online in 2026 face delays tied to power availability, and Britt Burt of Industrial Info Resources said the old focus on location has given way to speed to power. Burt estimated about $6 trillion is eyed for new data centers worldwide, with about $4 trillion of it in the US, while Denis said communities near big clusters in Virginia, Texas and Georgia have reportedly seen electricity rates rise 8 to 15%.

stories.Headline: Schneider Electric Unveils Modular Power Systems for AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
Schneider Electric said on October 23 that it had unveiled a new line of Prefabricated Power Modules and Power Skids for artificial intelligence data centers. Both products are built on a reference design the company co-developed with Nvidia, and Schneider says they can be used to build out power infrastructure in as little as six months. The idea is to manufacture power equipment in a factory in advance, rather than installing individual pieces at the data center site, which shortens construction time. Seoul Economic Daily reported the announcement, which comes as high-performance graphics processors push up electricity demand at data centers.

The reference design targets Nvidia's GB300 NVL72 system and supports power density of up to 142 kilowatts per rack. It combines power management with liquid cooling controls so that power and cooling equipment can run efficiently in environments packed with dense AI servers. The power modules use Schneider's Galaxy VXL uninterruptible power supply technology and come in three capacities, 2 megawatts, 2.25 megawatts and 2.5 megawatts. The 2.5-megawatt version is the largest single-container prefabricated power solution the company has released so far. Capacity can also be expanded by adding modules, so operators can start with initial demand and scale up in stages as they add GPU servers.

Schneider plans to supply the products to large hyperscale data centers, to neoclouds that provide AI-dedicated cloud services, and to colocation data centers that host servers for several companies. A Schneider official said that securing the necessary power infrastructure quickly and reliably is critical to scaling AI data centers. The official added that by applying the design developed with Nvidia, the company aims to help customers handle high-density AI environments and expand their equipment as power needs change. The products will be designed, manufactured and tested at the company's production facility in Sant Boi de Llobregat, near Barcelona, Spain, which Schneider recently expanded to meet rising demand for modular data center infrastructure.

On timing, the products will launch first in Europe, with supply widening to North America during 2026 and then rolling out to other regions, including Asia-Pacific. Separately, on October 22, Schneider announced a strategic collaboration with Nvidia and HPE to bring Physical AI to process industries, introducing what the companies call Industrial AI Agents at the Edge. Built on HPE Private Cloud AI, the agents run inside industrial environments and are meant to address data sovereignty, cybersecurity and AI consumption costs. The first three agents cover operational technology monitoring, cybersecurity and energy optimization. Gwenaelle Huet, Schneider's Executive Vice President for Industrial Automation, said the companies are combining expertise in automation, AI and edge computing to help customers turn operational data into action.

stories.Headline: SpaceX profit beats estimates on 161% revenue jump, growth in AI, satellite internet businesses
stories.Summary:
SpaceX reported third-quarter results on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, saying revenue for the three months ended in September rose 161 percent from a year earlier. The company, led by Elon Musk, posted net income of $4.4 billion, far above analysts' average projection of $1.88 billion and a turnaround from a loss of about $1.05 billion in the same period last year. The report was only its second quarterly disclosure since going public in June, and it marked a return to profit after a loss in the quarter ending in June. Shares rose as much as 4.7 percent in after-hours trading, with one outlet putting the price at about $153.30.

The AI business, now called Super Intelligence, was the biggest driver, with revenue of $7.56 billion, more than nine times the figure a year ago. Its operating income came in at $431 million, swinging from a loss of $1.7 billion a year earlier. SpaceX has become a major compute and infrastructure supplier to Anthropic and Alphabet, and in August it bought Cursor, the maker of an AI coding tool. Wider adoption of Grok, the language models built by xAI, also helped.

Starlink, the company's biggest income generator, ended the quarter with 13.6 million subscribers, short of the 14.2 million analysts had expected. Even so, revenue from the connectivity business rose 69 percent to about $5.25 billion, which still beat forecasts. One report put that segment's operating income at $2.37 billion, up 99 percent, and said average monthly revenue per user fell from $83 to $69 because of cheaper plans meant to support international growth. The space segment, covering rocket launches, grew only 6 percent to $1.77 billion and posted a small operating loss of $7 million, reflecting heavy spending on the Starship rocket.

Musk founded SpaceX and serves as its chief executive, and the company's market value of roughly $2 trillion rivals several megacap firms and tops Tesla. The stock was sold in a record-setting offering in June at $135 a share and closed Tuesday at $147.79, after a volatile stretch. Musk's plans include data centers in space and a rapidly reusable Starship, which the reports describe as costly, risky and likely to take years, though Wall Street remains largely bullish given his record of shaking up mature industries. A day before the earnings, Musk said he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America next year, a pledge that one outlet estimated at nearly $11 billion. An analyst at Macquarie said investors would be listening for launch timing, terrestrial build plans and appetite for more spectrum, after Starlink bought nationwide low-band spectrum earlier this month.

stories.Headline: Polen Focus Growth Strategy Boosts Meta Platforms, Inc. (META) on AI Monetization Potential
stories.Summary:
Polen Capital, an investment management firm, released its third-quarter 2026 letter for the Polen Focus Growth Strategy, and it highlighted Meta Platforms as a holding it added to. The firm said it increased its Meta position after the launch of Meta Muse, the company's personal AI agent. The Portfolio returned 4.46% net of fees in the quarter, ahead of the Russell 1000 Growth Index, which gained 0.92%, a gap of 3.54 percentage points. Even so, its net return for the year to date was still negative at 8.11%, while the benchmark was up 6.30%. The letter was covered on October 23, 2026, by Insider Monkey in an article published through Yahoo Finance.

On the details of the letter, Polen said software and services holdings helped results, while semiconductor and other direct beneficiaries of AI spending suffered valuation pressure as investors questioned spending levels, financing and returns on infrastructure. The managers kept rebalancing toward companies with strong long-term growth, better current momentum and clearer demand. They started positions in selected semiconductor equipment, power infrastructure, payments and data-storage firms, and trimmed or sold others. On Meta, Polen said Muse gives the company another way to earn money from its heavy AI investment beyond its core advertising business. It pointed to more than 3 billion daily active users across Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp as a distribution advantage, with possible new revenue from subscriptions, transactions and agentic consumer uses.

The views in the article belong to the Polen managers, who said they remain constructive but cautious about persistent inflation, higher interest rates, energy costs and valuations, especially for companies whose earnings lie further in the future. They said they aim to hold a balanced mix of competitively advantaged companies that can withstand shifts in market leadership. A separate MarketScreener report dated October 22, 2026, said UBS believes Meta's AI monetization could lift revenue growth, and that UBS rates the stock a Buy. That same day, Mizuho Securities raised its price target on Meta to $950 from $750, and Wedbush Securities noted that Meta stayed quiet on its 2027 cost and capital spending projections.

On the market backdrop, Meta shares closed at about $648.85 on October 21, 2026, giving a market value near $1.65 trillion, and the stock had fallen 13.89% over one month. Its 52-week range ran from $520.26 to $779.82. On October 22, MarketScreener reported the shares near $645.32, down 7.48% on the day, as US equity indexes fell on renewed worries about AI spending after Meta's results. Reports that day also said Meta's credit risk indicator hit a record high on its expanded AI spending plan, and that Rhode Island sued Meta over alleged tolerance for scam advertising. Insider Monkey's data showed 254 hedge fund portfolios held Meta at the end of the second quarter, down from 262 in the previous quarter.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Technology Solutions, Inc. (AITX) Guides to Op Cash Breakeven Jan 2027
stories.Summary:
Artificial Intelligence Technology Solutions, Inc., the Detroit-based AI security company trading as AITX, reported results for its fiscal second quarter ended August 31, 2026, in a release dated October 21, 2026. The figures come from its Form 10-Q, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on October 20, 2026, and are reviewed but unaudited. The company said the quarter marked a return to both sequential and year-over-year revenue growth, along with a more diversified customer base than at any point in its history. It also said an expanded cost program targets monthly operating cash breakeven in January 2027.

Revenue came to $1,985,604, up 5% from $1,888,749 a year earlier and up 8% from $1,831,202 in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Device rental revenue rose 4% to $1,765,293, which was 89% of the total and an annualized run rate of roughly $7.1 million, while direct sales climbed 14% to $220,311. Revenue excluding the largest customer hit a record $1,627,444, up 61% from $1,010,243 a year ago and up 11% from $1,463,319 in the first quarter. Gross profit was $1,063,301, or 54% of revenue, after a $270,987 non-cash inventory write-down tied to a discontinued residential camera line, and excluding that charge it was $1,334,288, or 67%.

The largest customer began cutting its spending in December 2025 as part of its own cost reductions, and its revenue was $358,160 in the quarter, down 3% from the prior quarter after a 50% sequential drop in the first quarter. That customer made up 18% of total revenue, compared with 46% in the prior-year quarter. Operating expenses for the six months ended August 31, 2026 fell 5% to $7,636,884 from $8,066,193, and general and administrative costs dropped 6%, or $380,193, mainly because of lower salary and wage expense. The company noted that these results reflect only one month of the cost-reduction program it announced on August 3, 2026.

In a separate release on October 22, 2026, the company said its subsidiary Robotic Assistance Devices, known as RAD, had secured recent orders for twelve devices across its RIO Mini, ROSA and TOM product lines. These included five ROSA units ordered by a longstanding channel partner for a Midwest construction site, three ROSA units from a security services partner, two RIO Mini units for an existing construction customer, and two more TOM units from a global logistics customer. Troy McCanna, RAD's Chief Security Officer and Chief Revenue Officer, said orders like these are becoming routine, and that the company values every order, large or small. The company cautioned that orders do not confirm delivery, revenue or positive cash flow, and that its risk factors include a history of operating losses and its ability to continue as a going concern.

Tempus AI applies artificial intelligence to precision medicine, giving physicians tools for personalized care while also supporting the discovery and delivery of therapeutics. stories.Headline: UK, Nigeria deepen collaboration on AI governance, digital transformation
stories.Summary:
The United Kingdom and Nigeria have strengthened their cooperation on artificial intelligence governance and digital transformation after a series of engagements involving the British Standards Institution, known as BSI, and Nigerian government agencies. The centrepiece was an Executive Workshop on AI Governance and Standards, delivered by BSI with the National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, NCAIR, under the UK Government's Digital Access Programme. It brought together senior officials, regulators and technology practitioners, and ended with a reception in Abuja. Officials who completed the workshop were recognised at a close-out event at the Afreximbank Trade Centre.

Participants looked at how international standards can support responsible AI adoption, risk management and oversight, including ISO/IEC 42001 for AI management systems and ISO/IEC 23894 for AI risk management. The partnership now covers digital trade, AI governance, digital public infrastructure, cybersecurity and data protection, with room for more work on electronic waste management and e-health. The visit also included meetings with the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's Climate Finance team to assess electronic waste models and ways to deepen cooperation on digital trade standards. Separately, at the Build 2026 conference in Abuja, the Nigeria AI Collective called for an inclusive, locally driven approach to AI, aligned with the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy.

Grace Bell, First Secretary for Economic Partnerships and Digital at the British High Commission, said AI offers major opportunities but needs strong governance, institutions and trusted standards. She described standards as strategic enablers of innovation, investment, trade and public trust, and said the UK works with BSI, the National Information Technology Development Agency, the Standards Organisation of Nigeria and the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy. Dr Olubunmi Ajala, NCAIR's national coordinator, said the collaboration had moved beyond theory to build sovereign institutional capacity, and he called for a permanent cross-government Community of Practice. At Build 2026, Dr Osasuyi Dirisu, executive director of the Policy Innovation Centre, which hosts the Collective's secretariat, said the group brings together civil society, academia, innovation and policy expertise.

On infrastructure, Communications Minister Dr Bosun Tijani, speaking through Ajala at Build 2026, named inadequate electricity, slow internet and limited access to advanced chips and cloud infrastructure as the main obstacles to Nigeria's AI ambitions. He said chip makers release new products every three or six months, leaving Nigeria behind by the time it buys them, and that major cloud providers have placed orders years ahead that chip makers may struggle to fill. The government proposes a data park near the Egbin Power Station in Lagos, using about 60 per cent of the plant's reportedly unused capacity, to serve Nigeria and Togo and support digital infrastructure across West Africa. The British High Commission said the UK will keep working with BSI and Nigerian institutions on standards for trust, cybersecurity, data governance and interoperability, as Nigeria develops its AI ecosystem and expands digital services.
