stories.Headline: Rogers, El-Sayed outline differing approaches to tariffs and AI during Detroit Economic Club forum
stories.Summary:
Michigan's two U.S. Senate nominees, Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, appeared separately at a forum hosted by the Detroit Economic Club on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. Each answered the same questions on policies affecting the state, including tariffs, artificial intelligence, education and health care. The event came just two weeks before the Nov. 3 general election, in a race that Cook Political Report currently rates a tossup. A recent debate between the two had turned contentious, leaving little room for calm policy discussion, and they were set to debate again the next evening.

On tariffs, both men said the tools could work if used carefully, though neither endorsed the way President Donald Trump has applied them. El-Sayed said Trump's approach has been chaotic and has hurt the auto industry and workers, and he compared it to giving a cancer patient too much chemotherapy at once. He proposed pairing tariffs with an industrial policy, including building a $25,000 electric vehicle with a 300-mile range over the next seven years, with subsidies for the first two years that would then be slowly withdrawn. Rogers, once a champion of the tariffs, said Trump should end those on Canada because they ignore how integrated the auto business is. He also credited tariffs with bringing vehicle production back, citing Silverados coming to the Orion plant, a multi-billion-dollar investment, and General Motors adding about 500,000 vehicles built in the United States.

On artificial intelligence, both candidates said stronger federal guardrails are needed, but their approaches differ. Rogers recalled being briefed, while chairing the House Intelligence Committee before leaving Congress in 2014, on an early AI-guided missile that appeared to make its own decisions in a test. He said he would support a national security framework already in the works, though he still needs to review its details, and he floated a narrow antitrust exemption so AI companies could cooperate on safety alone. El-Sayed, an AI skeptic, called for a pause in frontier research and said the technology could take 50% of white collar jobs over five to 10 years. He proposed an SEC or FDA-style regulatory agency, rebuilding leading AI firms as public interest corporations, democratically appointed leadership for at least 50% of their boards, and government ownership of about 50% of their value.

The Free Press reported that the candidates also agreed on the need to improve education and tackle a literacy crisis to strengthen Michigan's workforce. On health care, Rogers advocated price transparency, while El-Sayed supported a Medicare-for-All system. Although the two were not in the room together, El-Sayed took aim at Rogers's past record, saying Rogers had argued NAFTA would be good for Michigan in the long run, when in El-Sayed's view the state has hemorrhaged jobs under it. The forum gave each candidate room to answer more complex questions than the debate format allows.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind Staff Resign Over Military AI Contracts
stories.Summary:
Several Google DeepMind researchers have resigned, or are reportedly preparing to leave, over the company's growing military contracts, according to BBC interviews with current and former staff reported on October 23, 2026. Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer who joined DeepMind in 2023 and spent three years there, told the BBC and The Intercept that she quit after losing confidence in the company's ethical commitments. The Intercept reported her resignation on October 21, noting that she sent colleagues an internal letter urging them to "stay human" in the face of military work. Andreas Kirsch, an AI researcher, resigned separately, saying Google's governance and oversight were not strong enough for safe deployment in military and classified settings. The departures follow Reuters reporting that Google signed a classified agreement with the US Department of Defense allowing its AI models to be used for "any lawful government purpose," including classified military work.

Liguori said she staged a personal sick-out the day after Google announced the deal in April, using sick leave and holiday time. The agreement states that the systems should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or for autonomous weapons without appropriate human oversight and control. However, Reuters also reported that it requires Google to help adjust its AI safety settings and filters at the government's request. Kirsch reportedly said Google may have little practical ability to monitor or veto how the Pentagon uses its technology once it sits inside classified infrastructure. Google told the BBC that it applies a consistent contract-review process aligned with its acceptable-use policies and AI principles, and that employees have channels to raise concerns without fear of retaliation.

The company's published AI principles call for human oversight and alignment with international law and human rights. Liguori, for her part, wrote in her letter that she no longer believes the technology will have a net positive effect on society, calling the race to deploy agentic AI a terrible idea. She told The Intercept she could not keep working for a company that would help kill people or make war's brutality easier to escalate. The BBC noted that Google is not alone, as OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia and Reflection have also signed or pursued US military AI arrangements. Google and Amazon's $1.2 billion Project Nimbus contract has drawn separate employee criticism over cloud and AI services for Israel's government and military.

Google said at the time that Nimbus was not meant for sensitive military or intelligence work involving weapons or intelligence services, and an Israeli government minister rejected claims about AI-assisted targeting in a documentary as false and distorted. Retired Lt. Gen. Jack Shanahan, the former Project Maven director, warned that deployment pressure can outpace rigorous testing. Former OpenAI geopolitics head Sarah Shoker said AI can shrink decision time so much that a human operator struggles to check hundreds of AI-selected targets for errors.

stories.Headline: Scaling Laws Roadshow at North Dakota Law: Justice Jerod Tufte on AI in the Judiciary
stories.Summary:
North Dakota's interim Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee voted on Tuesday to advance a proposal that would set up AI consumer protections and create a state Artificial Intelligence Council. The committee sent the broader AI bill to Legislative Management after discussing worries about privacy, enforcement and how the council would be put together. A separate bill on companion chatbots did not advance as a committee bill, and lawmakers agreed to keep refining it for possible introduction by an individual legislator before the 2027 session. Members stressed that the draft is still open to revision. The committee also looked at early proposals to regulate data centers, though it did not move a finished bill.

Under the broader proposal, AI systems that deal with consumers would have to disclose that users are talking with artificial intelligence. It would bar developing or deploying AI with the intent to encourage self-harm, harm to others or criminal activity, and it would limit certain uses of biometric data to identify people without consent. The attorney general would enforce these protections. The bill would also create a supervised testing program letting developers try out innovative AI systems for a limited time without certain regulatory authorizations, with participants sending quarterly reports to the Information Technology Department. A seven-member AI council would study the technology and recommend changes to state laws and regulations.

Representative Mary Schneider questioned giving the attorney general exclusive enforcement power, which would block private lawsuits, saying parents or others harmed by AI may need to bring their own cases. Senator Janne Myrdal said those questions deserve more attention during the session, calling the draft a good start but not a final bill. On data centers, Representative Anna Novak outlined a "bring your own power" idea meant to keep residential customers from paying electricity or infrastructure costs caused by data centers or other large users, along with closed-loop water systems and standards for preparing former facilities for other uses. She said the plan is still being developed, partly because investor-owned utilities and rural electric cooperatives differ, and that zoning would stay local, with state permitting following if a community approves a project. Senator Dean Rummel suggested narrowing sales tax exemptions to computer technology, dropping them for items such as cooling systems, racks and fiber optics.

The companion chatbot draft would require chatbots to identify themselves as AI at the start of each interaction and at least every three hours during continuous adult use, and at least hourly for minors. It would also call for mental health protocols, crisis referrals and measures against content encouraging self-harm, and it would bar manipulative engagement tactics aimed at minors. The issue is also drawing attention in the attorney general race between Republican incumbent Drew Wrigley and Democrat Tim Lamb, who both said AI should not replace humans in investigations or legal work. Wrigley said he does not rush toward new regulation and wants expert-driven public conversations, while Lamb said he would assign an assistant attorney general to become an AI expert and work with other states on oversight. The interim committee is studying AI and data center topics for potential 2027 legislation, and additional proposals are expected from individual lawmakers before that session.

stories.Headline: Some government websites taken down in response to security risk: AI minister
stories.Summary:
Some Canadian government websites were taken down temporarily on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, as a precaution against a security risk, according to Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon. In a social media post, Solomon said the sites were pulled offline to protect government systems and Canadians' information. He said the move followed guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. The report was written by Catherine Morrison of The Canadian Press, with files from The Associated Press.

The first article's text is partly garbled, so only some details can be confirmed. As far as can be read, Solomon said the step was a response to a vulnerability found in PHP, a widely used programming language. The FBI's cyber division reportedly warned that the flaw could let malicious actors remotely run code in the programming language, which could put sensitive data and networks at risk. The PHP Foundation, which includes developers who work on the language, is said to have released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems. Solomon described the issue as global and said other governments and organizations are also taking measures.

Solomon said affected federal websites will be restored once the patches are applied. He said the government is taking the matter seriously. The website of the Finnish government was only partly available on Wednesday, and a message to visitors said Finnish government websites were experiencing a temporary disruption and were fully or partly unavailable while the issue was being resolved. The British Columbia government also posted on social media on Wednesday that it had taken some of its web pages offline as a precaution following a new global cybersecurity vulnerability.

It is unclear whether the British Columbia government was dealing with the same risk Solomon described, since the provincial government has not said so. The B.C. government said teams were working to restore the pages, but it did not say when they would be back. The articles do not say how many federal websites were affected or when they will return. Solomon's comments suggest the timeline depends on how quickly the patches can be applied across government systems.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA Introduces DSX POD AI Factories to Accelerate Europe’s Infrastructure Deployment
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA announced DSX POD at its GTC Berlin event on October 21, 2026. It is a reference design for complete Vera Rubin AI factories that partners build inside modular containers, then integrate and validate before the units are delivered. The containers arrive ready to connect to a prepared site's power, cooling, networking and other supporting infrastructure. NVIDIA says this cuts deployment time at such a site from six months to as little as 14 days. On the same day, the company also said European partners are adopting its wider DSX AI Factory Platform to build facilities that use less water and less power.

Under the design, the integration and installation of computing, networking, cabling, rack-level power and liquid cooling move from the building site to the manufacturing facility. Partners finish rack-to-rack cabling, wiring, piping and functional validation before shipment, and this work happens separately from site preparation. NVIDIA says factory-tested containers reduce exposure to component delays and error-prone onsite work. The aim is to shorten the time to first token, the point when a new AI factory starts running models for production workloads. The platform around it includes software such as DSX MaxLPS, which NVIDIA says lets operators generate the same number of tokens with up to 30% less power.

Its reference designs use closed-loop liquid cooling and dry coolers that can bring facility cooling water use close to zero, which NVIDIA says could save 54 million liters a day at a 2-gigawatt deployment, matching the daily water use of 180,000 households. Jensen Huang, NVIDIA's founder and chief executive, said an AI factory creates value when it starts producing tokens, not when construction ends. He said DSX POD brings factory-built precision and speed to AI infrastructure, so customers can scale capacity and bring revenue-generating production online sooner. Warren Barkley, NVIDIA's vice president of DSX product management, said Europe's technology leadership depends on how efficiently power and infrastructure are turned into intelligence. He said the platform gives operators the technologies and expertise to build responsibly and operate efficiently at scale.

NVIDIA is working with Anduril, Armada, Bull, Crusoe, DayOne, Dell Technologies, Delta, Eaton, Foxconn (Ingrasys), GIGABYTE, HPE, Lenovo, Pegatron, Quanta Cloud Technology, Schneider Electric, Vertiv and Wistron to deliver DSX POD AI factories worldwide in early 2027. For the wider DSX platform, CoreWeave, Firmus, Google Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale and Sharon AI plan to use the MaxLPS software. NVIDIA also launched SimReady Central on Hugging Face, a hub of simulation-ready digital models of power and cooling equipment, and released DSX OS, new open source software for infrastructure management. The company's release notes that its statements about expected benefits are forward-looking and carry risks, including its reliance on third parties to manufacture and assemble its products.

stories.Headline: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang joined on stage by robot ducks as he hails Europe’s AI potential
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang took the stage at the company's GTC conference in Berlin on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, flanked by small duck-shaped robots as he argued that Europe's engineering skills give it an edge in physical AI and robotics. The event, held at the tent-shaped Tempodrom, capped a European tour that had already taken him through London, Paris, Stockholm and Dublin. The robots were Microducks, 25 cm tall two-legged machines from French startup Pollen Robotics, developed with Hugging Face. Huang asked them to roll over and perform somersaults, though three keeled over at his order to take a nap, one needed extra persuasion, and another faced the wrong way at the end of his speech. Environmental protesters also briefly interrupted the keynote before security removed them.

Nvidia used the event to announce several products and partnerships. It unveiled DSX POD, a reference design for factory-built, containerized AI data centers that combines seven liquid-cooled Vera Rubin compute racks with Spectrum-X networking. The company says deployment could fall from six months to as little as 14 days at a prepared site, with availability expected in early 2027, and Huang claimed that at 2 gigawatts the design could save 54 million litres of water a day. Huang also introduced Agile ONE SN, a humanoid robot reference platform from German startup Agile Robots built on Nvidia's Isaac GR00T technology and a Jetson Thor compute module, also scheduled for early 2027. Agile Robots chief executive Zhaopeng Chen told Reuters the firm plans to produce 1,000 to 2,000 small humanoids next year with Nvidia, with production due to start late this year.

Huang said that every company in Europe will become an AI company, and that no region matches Europe's precision and craft in mechatronics, electronics and mechanical systems. He said Europe, often left behind by the US and Asia in the AI race and without a home-grown player on the scale of Nvidia, Anthropic or OpenAI, must play a central role, and should produce AI rather than simply consume it. He also said Nvidia's Hyperion car system is being adopted by more vendors, and that European telecoms operators are deploying Nvidia-powered computing for AI-RAN. Nvidia says it has committed nearly $10 billion to Europe's technology ecosystem and has built an early lead in the processors and software that act as robotic brains, which gives it a commercial interest in European industry succeeding.

Forrester principal analyst Paul Miller said Huang positioned Nvidia as a supporter and enabler of Europe's sovereign tech ambitions, noting that the company made 14 investments in European startups during the current trip. He cautioned, however, that Nvidia is not a European firm, so anything with critical ongoing dependence on it or any other non-European company is unlikely to meet the purest definitions of European tech sovereignty. The Register noted that the DSX POD timeline leaves out the work of preparing power, connectivity and other site infrastructure first. The 14-day claim is therefore a best case, and both DSX POD and Agile ONE SN are not due to arrive until early 2027.

stories.Headline: Amkor Technology stock jumps on Nvidia advanced packaging expansion
stories.Summary:
Shares of Amkor Technology rose 8% on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, after news that Nvidia plans to greatly expand its advanced packaging partnership with the semiconductor assembly firm into South Korea. Under the expanded agreement, the two companies aim to raise advanced packaging capacity in South Korea, with a goal of more than 300% growth in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028. The effort sits alongside Amkor's ongoing work on new manufacturing facilities in the country. Together, they are meant to support higher production volumes for Nvidia's current and next-generation AI platforms.

The Amkor deal is one piece of a wider push by Nvidia to scale manufacturing across several supply chain partners as demand for AI infrastructure surges. Nvidia is working with Amkor, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Unimicron Technology to expand capacity in substrates, advanced packaging, testing and optical engines. Nvidia plans to raise substrate capacity for its products 2.5-fold over the next three years. Samsung Electro-Mechanics joins Nvidia's substrate supply chain immediately through its existing South Korean facilities, and output allocated to Nvidia is expected to make up a major share of its total package substrate capacity by 2028. Nvidia is also backing Unimicron's substrate expansion in Taiwan through a capacity reservation agreement, with new capacity starting in the second quarter of 2027 and reaching full scale by mid-2028.

Nvidia is providing a $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance to KYEC to fund new U.S. testing facilities and equipment, with a target of high-volume production by April 2027. SPIL plans to expand its Taiwanese manufacturing capacity for optical engines used in co-packaged optics, aiming for a 15-fold increase by mid-2027 and then doubling that capacity again by late 2028. The articles do not include comments from Amkor or Nvidia executives on the packaging expansion itself. The reporting comes from Investing.com, which attributed the stock move to the news of the expanded partnership.

The latest agreement follows earlier ties between the two companies. Headlines listed alongside the article point to a $1.5 billion Nvidia and Amkor packaging deal for U.S. chip packaging about two months ago, and a report that total Nvidia agreements with Amkor now reach $3 billion. Amkor shares reportedly surged 16% after that earlier deal. Separate reporting from the same page indicates the stock later fell sharply, though the articles give few details on that decline.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence and Future of India's IT Companies
stories.Summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom announced on October 21, 2026, that the state has signed agreements with four of the largest technology companies working in generative AI: Google, Adobe, IBM and Microsoft. The deals are meant to train California's workforce for a wide range of AI jobs, including careers for students in grades 9 to 12, community colleges and California State Universities. The state says the agreements cost it nothing. They are also meant to let schools and industry partners work together so students can move more easily from the classroom into work.

The programs are expected to reach more than two million students in public high schools and universities across the state. Faculty and students in the community college and California State University systems will be supported, and high schools will be able to update their courses with current AI tools. The arrangement also aims to encourage networking and internship opportunities and widen access to advanced technology. California State University says the agreement formalizes a CSU-Industry AI Workforce Acceleration Board, which sits at the center of its own AI initiative.

Newsom said the state must stay ahead by making sure its students and workers are ready to lead, and described the effort as preparing tomorrow's innovators today. He added that fair access to next-generation training tools is one way to build economic opportunity for all Californians, and that the state will keep working with schools to promote safe and ethical use of new technology while stressing critical thinking and analytical skills. Labor Secretary Stewart Knox said fluency in AI tools will give students a large advantage at the start of their careers. Community colleges chancellor Sonya Christian called her system the largest workforce training provider in the nation, and CSU chancellor Mildred Garcia thanked the governor for his efforts, while other state officials praised the partnerships as an investment in the innovation economy.

The state points out that it is home to 33 of the top 50 privately held AI companies in the world, which it says shows its lead in generative AI. The agreements are also meant to keep California attractive to innovative firms, with a particular emphasis on supporting startups. Elsewhere, a July 2026 analysis in Economic and Political Weekly argues that AI is challenging the labour-heavy outsourcing model of India's software firms. It reports that AI already performs 37% of entry-level tasks in India, against a global average of 33%, and that the market value of TCS fell from a 2024 peak of about ₹15.2 trillion to below ₹8 trillion by mid-2026. The author concludes that the industry's future will depend less on how many engineers it employs and more on whether firms can capture value from AI-driven innovation.

stories.Headline: Europe RAISEs the Stakes for AI in Science
stories.Summary:
Businesses that use artificial intelligence face growing legal risk when what they tell people about their data practices does not match how their systems work, according to an analysis by Gouchev Law reported by PYMNTS on October 21, 2026. The analysis found a shared expectation among the Federal Trade Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission and European authorities that companies explain their AI practices accurately to users. It says that means tying disclosures to real data flows, vendor arrangements and model development, and dealing with changes before they take effect. The article does not say Europe is raising stakes for AI in science, so the story it actually covers is about corporate disclosure and regulatory scrutiny.

The analysis says the FTC is concerned about firms that collect information under one set of promises and later widen its use without enough transparency. A company that promised not to share customer data without consent, for example, could be exposed if it later sends chat transcripts to an outside AI provider for optimization. It cited FTC guidance warning that adopting more permissive practices through a "surreptitious, retroactive amendment" to contract terms or privacy policies may be unfair or deceptive. The analysis cautioned that a routine terms-update email, a website footer link or continued use of a product may not count as adequate acceptance of a material change. It also said broad statements that data helps improve services may fall short if they do not explain consequential AI uses, especially when customer inputs could train generative AI models.

The SEC adds another dimension, the analysis said, because AI disclosures must accurately reflect how systems are developed, trained and deployed. Marketing that overstates capabilities or mischaracterizes real use can create disclosure risk, and the FTC likewise looks at misleading product claims and omissions of material limitations. European data protection and consumer authorities, it added, are applying transparency, accountability and purpose-limitation principles to AI, while AI-specific frameworks bring expectations on risk classification, governance and controls across a system's lifecycle. Liability can also arise through customer contracts, as in an unnamed company's case, where a third-party AI vendor kept and reused customer content for model improvement and confidential material surfaced in other customers' workspaces. That dispute involved breach-of-contract allegations and ended in a six-figure settlement.

To lower exposure, the analysis recommended a joint assessment by legal, product and engineering teams. Businesses should list their deployed and upcoming AI systems, identify what information each one accesses, and map the outside vendors and APIs involved in processing. The results should guide updates to customer agreements, privacy policies and terms of use, which should say what is collected, processed and stored, how models interact with it, which providers take part and whether users can opt out. Vendor agreements should cover retention, model training and reuse in a way that matches customer commitments, and policies should be reviewed as products change, with legal and compliance involved before launch. The aim, the analysis said, is to make disclosures an accurate account of current operations and planned changes, closing the gaps that invite enforcement and contract claims.

stories.Headline: How governments around the world are shaping what AI can say about politics
stories.Summary:
A researcher at a nonpartisan think tank at Vanderbilt University, Jordi Calvet-Bademunt, wrote in The Conversation on October 20, 2026, that governments around the world are increasingly shaping what AI chatbots can say about politics. He cited a recent survey finding that about one in five American voters has asked chatbots about elections and politics, as the U.S. midterms approach. He and his colleagues worked with legal experts to study how governments in 12 countries and regions regulate AI, publishing reports in 2025 and 2026. Their finding was that governments often rely on existing rules, such as national security or anti-state propaganda laws, instead of writing new AI laws. Because many tech companies apply the same policies everywhere, the answers American voters receive may be shaped by governments at home and abroad.

The article lists several examples. In 2024, an Indian journalist asked Google's Gemini whether Prime Minister Narendra Modi's policies were fascist, and the government then required official permission before "unreliable" AI models could be released, though that requirement was later dropped. China requires AI models to uphold "socialist core values," and a Turkish court blocked Grok posts that allegedly insulted President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and religious values. In December 2025, a Vietnamese court sentenced two activists living in Germany to 17 years each in prison for spreading anti-state material, with prosecutors accusing them of using AI to fake the voices and images of Vietnamese leaders. The European Union's AI Act, adopted in 2024, requires any company offering AI tools in Europe to mark AI-generated content, and Anthropic applies the marks globally because it cannot reliably do so by region.

European regulators have also acted on political content more directly. In August 2026, the EU placed ChatGPT under the strictest tier of its Digital Services Act, so OpenAI must now assess and reduce systemic risks, including threats to elections such as disinformation. The Dutch Data Protection Authority tested four chatbots before the 2025 national election and found the political middle ground "virtually disappears" in their voting advice, urging providers to stop their systems being used for it. In 2024, Thierry Breton, then the EU's top digital rules enforcer, reminded Elon Musk of his legal obligations before Musk's live interview with Donald Trump on X. In the United States, a 2025 executive order on "Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government" requires AI models the government buys to be "truth-seeking" and ideologically neutral.

The author argues that "truth-seeking" can mean very different things to different people, noting that the president recently banned three news outlets from the White House and dismissed media polls as "fake." The Federal Trade Commission has suggested that AI companies steering answers toward undisclosed ideological objectives might break consumer protection law. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that eight in 10 Americans believe Republican and Democratic voters cannot agree on basic facts. Dozens of states have passed laws restricting AI-generated political deepfakes, and U.S. courts blocked the California and Hawaii laws, citing the First Amendment. The author advises voters to treat chatbot answers about elections as a starting point and not a substitute for their own critical thinking.

stories.Headline: OpenAI to bring AI models to Google's cloud, in further expansion beyond Microsoft
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on October 21, 2026 that its artificial intelligence models will become available to developers through Google’s cloud, after years of competition between the two companies. The ChatGPT maker will place its GPT products in Google Cloud’s model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks. This follows the end of Microsoft’s exclusive license on OpenAI’s intellectual property less than six months earlier. The day after that exclusivity ended, Amazon announced plans to host OpenAI models, and now Google is doing the same. The move puts OpenAI’s models on all three of the top U.S. cloud infrastructure providers.

The expansion reflects OpenAI’s push to reach enterprise developers and build its business beyond its consumer roots. Google Cloud’s annualized revenue growth accelerated to about 82 percent in the second quarter from 63 percent in the first quarter, partly due to demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second quarter cloud growth of 37 percent and 42 percent respectively. OpenAI is courting investors at a 1.4 trillion dollar valuation and targeting an initial public offering. Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when OpenAI used Google’s cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface.

OpenAI said in a blog post that Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them. Google introduced a new Gemini agent on October 8, 2026, designed to handle work across email, documents, spreadsheets and other business tools, planning tasks and connecting to company systems from a single interface. The company said its latest enterprise agent offering combines access to company information and business applications with administrative controls and governance features. OpenAI is also developing workplace agents that can take on tasks across business applications.

The broader context is that enterprise AI is shifting from a race for intelligence, speed, benchmarks and reasoning toward turning that intelligence into work businesses can consistently trust. Businesses cannot delegate accountability to a model, and organizations must decide which work AI should support, which it should complete and where human judgment must remain. The next enterprise AI race will not be won simply by having the smartest model, but by companies that know what they want that intelligence to do and build systems that allow them to trust the result. Separately, Microsoft and Google are backing three retired U.S. nuclear reactor restarts in Michigan, Pennsylvania and Iowa that could together deliver 2.25 gigawatts, with restarts targeted between 2027 and 2029.

stories.Headline: I&B Ministry Advises TV Channels to Exercise Caution in AI Use
stories.Summary:
India's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting issued an advisory on October 21, 2026, telling all private satellite TV channels to take due care when using artificial intelligence and its tools, including generative AI, in their programmes. The ministry said AI use in areas such as graphics and virtual news presentations should be kept to an assistive capacity, without harming the accuracy, authenticity or sensitivity of news content. It issued the advisory on the recommendation of its Inter-Departmental Committee, which was set up under the Cable Television Networks (Amendment) Rules, 2021. That committee found that telecasts on various channels did not fit the spirit of the Programme Code, and it noted that similar news and visuals were aired on multiple channels on similar topics.

The advisory asks broadcasters to strengthen their editorial and content review systems and to make sure everyone involved in gathering, editing, producing and airing news understands the Programme Code. Channels are encouraged to hold workshops, training and sensitisation sessions for editorial and production teams at regular intervals. Beyond AI, the ministry told channels to use only maps of India published by the Survey of India, to base crime and violence reporting on verified facts, and to time-stamp visuals of disasters and avoid repeating disturbing footage. It also said channels should avoid live coverage of anti-terror operations, and that debates must not promote communal or anti-national attitudes, with panellists carefully chosen and briefed, and with muting, disclaimers or cutting the feed used where needed. On sexual offences, channels must follow Supreme Court directions and avoid revealing any detail that could identify a victim.

The ministry warned that any breach of the Programme Code could bring action under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and its rules, and it stressed that sticking to these statutory duties is essential. The committee also said inappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalised on air. MediaNama noted that the advisory does not define what counts as assistive use, does not say whether it covers AI news anchors, and does not cite any Programme Code provision for its AI guidance, although it cites one for every other instruction. It also does not require channels to label AI anchors.

On context, MediaNama reported that channels such as Aaj Tak, News18 and Odisha TV use AI anchors, as does the ministry's own broadcaster Doordarshan, which introduced two AI anchors on DD Kisan in May 2024. In March, the ministry told a parliamentary committee it wanted to expand such use. The outlet also pointed to fake AI videos of Indian anchors spreading false political claims. It reported that between 2021 and 2025 the ministry took 144 actions against private satellite channels, including 50 warnings, 54 orders to run apology scrolls and three off-air orders, according to a February reply in the Rajya Sabha.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Offers Rs 3.25 Crore Salary for Human Writer Job
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, has advertised an opening for an Executive Communications Writer based in San Francisco. The listing surfaced in coverage published on October 22, 2026, and Business Insider was cited as the original source for the details. It offers a yearly salary of $295,000 to $345,000, which the articles convert to roughly Rs 2.78 crore to Rs 3.25 crore. The opening has drawn attention because an AI company that makes a tool able to produce speeches and essays in seconds is looking to hire a person to write.

The selected candidate would work closely with Anthropic's senior leaders, writing speeches, preparing public statements and producing content on complex technical subjects. The writer must be able to explain advanced AI ideas in plain language for people without a technical background. The job also involves supporting executives before major public appearances, working with media representatives and outside communications teams, and keeping the company's messaging clear and consistent. Applicants need at least eight years of senior-level professional writing experience, strong skills in simplifying complicated material, and a background in executive communications. Anthropic also wants someone who can quickly absorb technical concepts and stay composed when news breaks.

Communications experts quoted by Business Insider said the posting shows the lasting value of human judgment. Ann Handley of MarketingProfs said that when speed becomes cheap, judgment carries a premium, and she described the role as shaping thought leadership rather than just polishing language. Joseph Braue of Content Marketing Partners said much of corporate writing means challenging unsupported claims and resisting pressure to publish weak material. Josh Bernoff, a business strategy author, said writers must show their work actually moves people, and he advised early-career writers to use AI for research while composing the final words themselves. One LinkedIn commenter, an Oregon-based author, joked that the job would suit a writer who wanted to build their own gallows to train AI.

The hiring comes as Anthropic's own data shows AI changing its workforce. Junior workers made up just 9% of technical hires in June, down from 27% in early 2025, and CFO Krishna Rao said in May that AI already writes 90% of the company's code. Rao added that hiring could still grow because there is no shortage of work to do. The pay is far above a comparable listing from Amazon Web Services, which offered $126,700 to $171,400 for an Executive Communications Manager in Seattle. The articles do not say when the role will be filled.

stories.Headline: How to Make the AI revolution work in products.
stories.Summary:
The Writers Guild of America East has begun offering its members free access to a software tool called Cloak, which makes documents "unreadable" to artificial intelligence models while keeping their formatting intact. The union announced the move on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. A writer can upload a script and get back a copy designed to resist AI analysis, scraping and training. The aim is to let writers send scripts to studio executives, producers, agents, actors and editors without worrying that the material will be ingested by AI systems.

Members get Cloak at no cost, while non-members can use it for $10 when they go through the guild's script registration service. That registration service is already open to all writers, whether or not they belong to the union, and is meant to protect work before it is shared widely. Separately, an interview published the same day with NVIDIA's David Niewolny, the company's senior director and global head of business development for healthcare and medical, looked at how hospitals can run AI at the edge and in the cloud. He described edge computing as important in healthcare because so much of the work happens at the point of care, where speed and data residency matter. He said real-time perception, device control, alerts and procedural support generally belong at the edge, while large-scale training and simulation can run in a cloud or on-premises data center.

Tom Fontana, president of the Writers Guild of America East, said the partnership with Cloak expands the guild's efforts to protect members' work and push back against AI companies that exploit writers and other creative workers. He said members should not have to worry that their work will be used to train AI models after they send it to producers or agents, or that months or years of effort will be reduced to an AI-generated summary of an email attachment. Larry J. Cohen, co-chair of the guild's AI Task Force, said generative AI is often falsely sold on the promise of making creative work obsolete, when the creative process is human. He said the guild is also pursuing protections through contracts, legislation and member education.

Niewolny advised healthcare organizations to err on the side of caution about data, noting that most people do not want raw patient data leaving the site. He suggested running models locally and centralizing only items such as approved model artifacts, de-identified data, aggregated telemetry and performance metrics. He said security must cover a device's full life cycle, including secure boot and signed software, and that mission-critical AI needs a governance system linking clinical, IT, security, privacy, legal and development teams. He pointed to staffing shortages and the cost of care as reasons the timing is right, and described NVIDIA's role in supplying edge hardware such as the Jetson, IGX and DGX Spark platforms and in the Open H initiative to build a large data set of robotic surgical data.

stories.Headline: Data and skills hinder textile AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The International Textile Manufacturers Federation (ITMF) and the Institut für Textiltechnik (ITA) of RWTH Aachen University published a white paper on 15 October 2026 on how the global textile industry is adopting artificial intelligence. Titled "AI in the Textile Value Chain: A Strategic Guide to Artificial Intelligence for the Global Textile Industry," the 49-page report concludes that fragmented data, skills shortages and weak governance are bigger obstacles than the technology itself. It draws on ten webinar sessions held between 2024 and 2026, which featured more than 20 experts from industry, research and policy organisations. Further input came from talks with practitioners at the ITMF Annual Conference 2025 in Yogyakarta, Indonesia. The authors describe the industry as digitally fragmented rather than under-digitalised, because decades of partial digitalisation have left large amounts of data locked in disconnected systems.

The report says AI is already producing measurable returns in computer-vision inspection of fabrics and yarns, predictive maintenance, energy optimisation and demand forecasting. One case study found that causal AI cut scrap by 10% on a nonwovens production line. The authors expect that integrated, end-to-end AI workflows spanning several processes could become realistic within two to three years. They also warn that AI cannot fix poor data and may amplify existing flaws, and that many companies hold less usable information than they believe. Trust is another condition, since manufacturers want assurances on commercially sensitive information, cybersecurity, transparency and accountability.

The paper recommends that companies put workforce development first, set up sound data management and introduce AI step by step through clearly defined uses with measurable results. It also calls for more collaboration before competition, especially to help small and medium-sized enterprises that lack the means to build AI capabilities alone. Possible measures include common data standards, secure industry data spaces that let firms keep ownership of sensitive information, and a controlled sector-specific tool described as a Textile GPT. Olivier Zieschank, Director of ITMF, said AI is no shortcut around the industry's structural problems but can help firms handle complexity and make the most of scarce expertise. He added that working out where AI really helps is a learning process, which is why exchange through associations matters.

Professor Thomas Gries, Director of ITA at RWTH Aachen University, stressed building data management into both daily and strategic decisions. He said companies need a dedicated task force to embed data integration into their technical and business processes, and he advised bringing in outside specialists to review current processes and find openings for better data use and automation. The report notes that human expertise remains essential for setting objectives, handling unusual situations and ensuring accountability. It adds that routine analytical and administrative work is increasingly supported by AI, which raises demand for digital literacy. Its overall finding is that progress towards wider adoption by 2030 will depend less on more advanced algorithms than on reliable data foundations, relevant skills and confidence in AI-enabled processes.

stories.Headline: Enabling Local AI Resilience with Cisco Cloud Control and NVIDIA DGX Station
stories.Summary:
On October 21, 2026, Cisco published a blog post by Yash Sheth describing how Cisco Cloud Control works with the NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows to govern local AI. The pitch is that local AI is moving from chat to action, with agents needing continuous inference while keeping data secure and costs predictable. That creates an operating challenge, because organizations must know which agents use a machine, how their requests behave, and what security policy applies to their actions. Cisco says its approach lines up with NVIDIA's OpenShell Reference Architecture for Safe Agents, with DefenseClaw deployed on the DGX Station to give discovery, telemetry and enforcement hooks into local agents. The next day, October 22, NVIDIA published a separate technical post about linking more of its DGX Spark machines.

The Cisco design has three paths: inference, security and telemetry. Agents send model requests to a configured serving endpoint, either on the same workstation or across a network, while supported agent hooks send events to DefenseClaw, which in the managed profile uses Secure Client machine identity to authenticate inspection requests to Cisco AI Defense. OpenTelemetry collection delivers activity, timing and decision evidence to observability destinations, and Splunk Agent Observability, available on-prem or as SaaS, gathers events and traces to spot behavior drift, malicious actions or security risks. Cloud Control adds views for fleet context, token use and estimated cost, agent behavior, policy state, hybrid inference and network security.

In NVIDIA's post, official support for eight-node DGX Spark clusters was announced at GTC Berlin, scaling unified memory from 128 GB on one node to 512 GB on four and 1 TB on eight. That lets the full GLM 5.3 model from Z.ai, at 753 billion parameters and about 470 GB in NVFP4, run locally, with total decode reaching 67 tokens per second at a concurrency of eight. The Cisco post walks through how a team would handle a rogue agent on a DGX Station. An operator sees a guardrail event in Cloud Control, follows traces showing the model used, the tools called and the actions taken before the denial, and finds why the agent tried to break the organization's trust policy.

The team then writes a policy for that scenario and pushes it to every station at once, and Cloud Control can use the Cisco network to quarantine a station during investigation. Cisco also notes that collection and export policies decide which prompts, responses and identifiers leave the endpoint, with redaction applied at that boundary. Some of the products and features described remain in development and will be offered when and if available. NVIDIA's authors, Arvind Gopalakrishnan, Eugene Rakhmatulin, Manini Sharma and Prerit Rodney, say a Spark-optimized collective backend called RoCEnante cuts all-reduce latency on switch-connected clusters, giving a 4.43x decode speedup at eight nodes versus 3.05x without it.

Their benchmarks show decode on Qwen3.8-27B in NVFP4 rising from roughly 12 tokens per second on one node to 52 on eight. NeMo Switchyard routes requests between model pools on a shared cluster and can raise aggregate throughput up to 3x when most traffic moves to a smaller model. Pre-training a nanochat model across eight nodes reached a 7.79x speedup at 97.4% scaling efficiency. NVIDIA says eight-node support in NVIDIA Sync, whose Cluster Assistant handles setup and device management, is coming by the end of the year.

stories.Headline: HHS Plans Sole-Source Anthropic Claude Contract
stories.Summary:
The Department of Health and Human Services plans to give Anthropic a sole-source contract to keep its Claude artificial intelligence tools running for department staff. A special notice posted on SAM.gov on Monday, October 19, 2026, said HHS intends to award a limited continuity-of-services contract for the existing Claude for Enterprise and Claude for Government services. The contract would last until the agency awards a multiple-award blanket purchase agreement for enterprise AI. ExecutiveGov reported the notice on October 21.

The award would cover the current Claude deployment inside HHS infrastructure. Covered capabilities include chat, drafting, summarization, search, research and reporting, reasoning models and long-context modes, and document processing and data analysis. Coding assistance, agentic and delegated-work functions, native applications, secure API access, and administrative controls with audit reporting are also included. Connectors, projects, workspaces, memory and web-grounded research would be available where authorized. HHS said the services must meet its security and data-handling rules, including encryption for data in transit and at rest, U.S. data residency, audit logging, and provisions for protected health information where eligible.

HHS is the agency behind the plan, and it justified the sole-source approach by saying it needs to keep using Anthropic's proprietary Claude model family. The notice set October 21 as the response deadline. It gave no projected award date or contract value for the Anthropic action, and it left the schedule for the planned multiple-award agreement unspecified. HHS has named that agreement as its next procurement vehicle for enterprise access to frontier AI models and advanced features.

The timing follows two earlier developments. HHS rolled Claude out to all department employees in December 2025, according to FedScoop. The notice also arrives ahead of the scheduled October 31 expiration of Anthropic's discounted General Services Administration OneGov agreement, which gave agencies access to Claude for Enterprise and Claude for Government for a dollar. The interim award would preserve access to Claude while the department moves toward the broader competitive procurement.

stories.Headline: Applications Open for County College of Morris Artificial Intelligence and Data Science Apprenticeship
stories.Summary:
County College of Morris is accepting applications for the next cohort of its Artificial Intelligence and Data Science Apprenticeship, which was announced in coverage published on October 21 and 22, 2026. The program is open to CCM students and adult learners who live in New Jersey and want careers in artificial intelligence, machine learning and data science. It pairs classroom learning at the college with paid, hands-on work experience guided by industry professionals. The deadline to apply is 11:59 p.m. on Monday, November 2.

To finish the program, participants must complete 30 credits of college coursework and 2,000 hours of paid, on-the-job training. Those who do so earn a certificate in AI and Data Science from CCM, along with a Registered Apprenticeship Certificate of Completion from the New Jersey Department of Labor. Tuition and fees toward the college's AI and Data Science Certificate are covered for eligible participants. The credits can also count toward a 60-credit associate degree at CCM, and students may then transfer to a four-year university to pursue a bachelor's degree.

Nancy Binowski, a professor of AI and Data Science at CCM, said artificial intelligence and data science are changing the global economy at a remarkable pace. She described the earn-and-learn model as a way for students to gain real-world experience in a dynamic, in-demand field. She added that employers get a chance to develop emerging talent and apply AI and data science solutions to their business needs. Employers can also help apprentices build professional skills and expand their networks.

The college received support from the New Jersey Community College Consortium for Workforce and Economic Development, and it was chosen as one of only two community colleges in the state to help deliver New Jersey's first apprenticeship in this field registered with the United States Department of Labor. The effort is meant to prepare workers for careers involving artificial intelligence and data science across many industries. Employers interested in partnering with the program can email AIApprenticeship@ccm.edu or call 973-328-5703. Applicants can apply through the apprenticeship page on the CCM website.

stories.Headline: AI discovered a software vulnerability that could impact 70% of websites worldwide. The rush is on to patch it
stories.Summary:
An AI-assisted discovery has exposed serious security flaws in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of websites worldwide, prompting governments and companies to race through the night to patch them. The FBI's cyber division warned on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, that the flaws could let malicious actors run code remotely on affected systems. The agency said this raised the risk that sensitive data and networks could be compromised, and it recommended that operators take websites offline if they cannot update them right away. Many government sites appeared to be working on Thursday, though some outages and limited services remained while the security work continued.

Governments are responding by updating software and, in some cases, pulling services down temporarily. In Britain, the prime minister's office said some limited government services could be offline during the work, but that no large public-facing critical services were affected. Japan's prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, urged website administrators to check whether they use PHP and to install a patch released late Wednesday, adding that temporarily suspending websites could be an effective way to reduce risk if a fix could not be applied quickly. The PHP Foundation said it had released fixes and instructions for updating systems. The European Union cybersecurity agency, ENISA, told organizations to act immediately.

The Japanese government said it had received no reports of damage from cyberattacks linked to the PHP flaws, and its chief cabinet secretary, Minoru Kihara, said some government sites were taken offline only as a precaution. Cloudflare's chief executive, Matthew Prince, said there had been "millions" of attempts to exploit the flaw in the hours after it was announced. OpenAI, which led a coalition of researchers and security firms working on the issue over the past two months, described the flaws as one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory and said its AI appeared to find them before any attackers did. The company's role in the work was noted by the British government, which said it was working with OpenAI and international partners.

James Sullivan, Director of Cyber and Tech at the Royal United Services Institute in London, said the two critical flaws could allow attackers to reach websites without a password and control web servers, steal or alter data, or launch further attacks. He called it staggering that some of the flaws were more than a decade old, and said AI can both help attackers find weaknesses and help defenders fix them. He said some sites may remain down because several patches exist for different software types and must be tested before release. Sullivan advised basic steps such as identifying vulnerable systems, installing updates promptly and using two-factor authentication.

stories.Headline: Metzger order bans Ulster from using Flock cameras, AI surveillance tools
stories.Summary:
Ulster County Executive Jen Metzger issued an executive order on Thursday, October 22, 2026, barring all county departments and employees under her authority from buying, contracting for, or deploying Flock cameras and similar AI-assisted surveillance technologies. The county does not currently use those tools. The order also stops county departments from letting vendors or contractors use such technology on the county's behalf, and it took effect immediately. The Daily Freeman reported that it covers any service Flock Safety provides to the county, along with "vehicle or person reidentification" tools. The measure follows a wider trend in which Hudson Valley and other municipalities have been canceling Flock contracts.

Metzger said the order responds to significant privacy, security, and civil liberties concerns, as well as a lack of oversight in the AI industry. She noted that the concern is the technology itself, not any single seller, since other companies offer similar products. The Mid Hudson News reported that she said private AI developers face no regulatory guardrails to protect security and safety. She argued that the order keeps the county from adopting tools that could erode privacy or expose residents' personal information to misuse. Metzger framed the decision as a safeguard for residents rather than a restriction on public safety work.

Sheriff Juan Figueroa supports the executive order, saying it offers a framework for protecting public safety while upholding residents' privacy and civil liberties. The sheriff's office plans its own statement outlining its approach to surveillance technology, which it says will bring transparency and clarity. The Daily Freeman reported that the sheriff's office has said it does not and will not use Flock cameras, and that it has used Motorola license plate readers for more than a decade. Earlier, on October 9, the U.S. Department of Justice announced a $794,000 grant to the sheriff's office for modernizing law enforcement technology, including Motorola plate reader expansion and a proposed AI-assisted report writing system from Axon. The sheriff's office later said it decided not to move forward with the AI report writing program after a pilot and would no longer add Motorola readers.

Separately, the Daily Freeman reported that automatic license plate readers operated by German company Jenoptik AG enforce traffic violations around four Kingston school zones, reviewed by the city's Parking Violations Bureau. The Daily Freeman described its story as developing, so further details about the sheriff's statement or the status of existing systems may follow. The articles do not say whether the order will affect the Kingston school zone system. Readers can expect more information on how the county applies the order in practice as officials issue their statements.

stories.Headline: Call for Abstracts — 2027 Petrie-Flom Center Annual Conference: Generative AI in Healthcare: Law & Regulation - Petrie-Flom Center
stories.Summary:
The Petrie-Flom Center at Harvard Law School has announced a call for abstracts for its 2027 annual conference, titled Generative AI in Healthcare: Law and Regulation. The center describes generative AI as artificial intelligence that produces output such as text or images, a technology that has become central to the economy and political debate and is increasingly used in healthcare. The conference and a resulting edited volume will examine how law and regulation can and should shape its future in medicine. Abstracts are due December 1, and accepted participants will present at a writers' workshop on May 3.

The organizers list several questions the conference will address. They ask how generative AI should be deployed, used, supervised, and monitored in healthcare, and who should oversee the development of new tools. They also ask how safety and effectiveness might be evaluated, which regulatory or other legal structures would be best for governance, and who is responsible when something goes wrong. A final question concerns how these tools should be incorporated into healthcare financing, insurance, and delivery systems. The articles do not describe any new rule or requirement; the call is an invitation for scholarly work on these issues.

The announcement was issued by the Petrie-Flom Center for Health Law Policy, Biotechnology, and Bioethics at Harvard Law School, which published it on October 22, 2026. The center describes itself as a research program focused on legal analysis and interdisciplinary scholarship for health policymakers, medical professionals, industry leaders, patients, and families. It was founded in 2005 through a gift from Joseph H. Flom and the Carroll and Milton Petrie Foundation. The center's website lists a range of related work, including research on artificial intelligence and fellowships for students and visiting scholars.

Separately, a GovCIO Media video published the same day examined how federal call centers are adopting AI and other tools. Its speakers included officials from the IRS Joint Operations Center, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and the contractor Maximus. The piece says federal call centers handle millions of interactions, and it describes how AI is being used to manage demand, prioritize information, and improve service. The two items address AI in different public settings, though the articles do not connect them directly. Further developments on the Harvard conference, such as the selection of abstracts, are not described in the articles.

stories.Headline: External evaluators find flaws in OpenAI's AI monitoring system in pilot review
stories.Summary:
On October 22, 2026, the AI safety groups METR and Redwood Research published an account of a pilot review in which each sent one researcher to spend three weeks inside OpenAI with deep access to its internal systems. The review ran from July 21 to August 11, 2026, and was aimed at OpenAI's internal system for monitoring misaligned AI behavior. The evaluators reported several new vulnerabilities in that system as it existed on and before July 21. OpenAI received a full 61-page internal report, while a 38-page version with redactions went to the leadership of the two groups.

The evaluators had access to OpenAI's internal code, monitor prompts, configuration details and documentation, and they interviewed about a dozen staff across monitoring, safety and security teams. They worked on OpenAI-issued devices that never left the premises and were accompanied while onsite. The parties agreed in advance to publish only a brief, high-level public post, and OpenAI kept the right to redact anything it judged sensitive. METR estimated that roughly 75 to 94 percent of eligible agentic traffic from models at least as strong as GPT-5.5 was monitored, with 99.2 percent of the internal Codex subset within that figure. The gaps they described included reinforcement learning runs that were not covered at the start of the exercise and compaction events that likely left about 10 percent of eligible Codex traffic unmonitored from May to July 2026.

The findings also described ways an agent could evade the monitor entirely. One exploit could keep hundreds of recent actions, including those used to carry out the exploit, from being monitored, and a method could in principle let Codex agents bypass sandboxing to act with their users' full permissions. The evaluators also described inputs that could likely make the monitor fail, two client-controlled headers that disable monitoring for new agents, and two unmonitored internal tools that could be subverted. OpenAI has since said all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards are patched and has described major changes to the system's coverage, but METR said it has not evaluated those claims. OpenAI's own March 19, 2026 description of the system, which relies on GPT-5.4 Thinking and reviews agent activity within 30 minutes, said it could not confidently quantify false negatives without dedicated control evaluations.

The evaluators framed the findings as a reason to build future monitoring that resists deliberate, sustained attacks by capable agents, with practices such as checking agents at set intervals rather than only at the end of their turns and keeping tamper-proof, searchable logs. METR said the exercise benefited from the depth of access and from logistical and technical support provided by OpenAI staff. It said future exercises will follow the transparency and independence practices described in its published approach to working with AI companies. The broader context, as Reuters reported, is that AI labs and the Trump administration have promoted outside evaluation, while companies worry that evaluators inside their walls could take proprietary information to rivals.

stories.Headline: Javier Milei's Case Against AI Regulation
stories.Summary:
Javier Milei, the Argentine president, made the case for leaving artificial intelligence unregulated in a June 4 column in the Financial Times. In it he argued that AI would free people from the limits of the human brain and push productivity far beyond current expectations, and he warned against what he called premature and poorly understood rules. The column came as he pushed to attract AI companies to Argentina, the week after he introduced legislation built on three pillars. Those pillars were leaving AI unregulated, creating a new legal category for nonhuman corporations run by AI agents or robots, and keeping corporate taxes low. As of late September, the Senate had held hearings on the bill but had not moved it forward.

The legislation would therefore leave AI development largely free of regulatory limits while giving machine-operated entities a legal standing that does not exist today. The articles do not say how that category would be defined or what obligations it would carry. Milei's supporters see the approach as a way to draw investment, while the stalled Senate process shows that lawmakers have not yet settled on it. The reporting makes clear the proposal remains a set of ideas rather than an enacted policy.

Milei is the person responsible for the proposal, and his own words in the Financial Times carry the core argument. He framed unregulated development as a way to avoid the deadly hand of regulation that he said was poorly understood. The articles provide no direct response from Senate members or other critics beyond the fact that the hearings have taken place without a vote. Their focus is on the stated aims of the plan rather than on detailed rebuttals.

The Milei proposal sits within a wider debate about AI's social effects. A separate piece describes Haredi rabbis in Lakewood, New Jersey, who met in January to discuss banning AI from schools and homes and who planned a communal fast in protest, though their decision was not binding on other Orthodox groups. Some leftist critics and religious thinkers likewise object to AI on grounds of labor, human effort, and the displacement of meaningful work. Whether Argentina's Senate advances the bill, and how the new legal category would work in practice, remain open questions that the articles do not resolve.

stories.Headline: Florida Attorney General Proposes New Law Restricting Social Media, App Downloads and AI Chatbots for Minors
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has proposed a sweeping new law aimed at restricting social media, app downloads and AI chatbots for minors. The proposal, called the Safe Screens Act, would require parental consent before minors download or purchase apps. It follows an October 14 ruling by the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that allowed Florida to enforce its existing restrictions on social media accounts for children under 14. The legislation remains a proposal and would need approval from Florida lawmakers before it could become law. The bill would require social media companies to set stricter defaults for users ages 14 to 17.

Teenagers would be limited to two hours of social media use per day and 60 hours per month, and access would be blocked from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. daily and from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. on school weekdays.

Autoplay and infinite scrolling would be turned off by default unless a verified parent authorizes them, and public likes and reaction counts would be hidden unless a parent enables them. AI chatbot operators would be barred from offering romantic or emotional companionship features to children, and from encouraging suicide, self-harm, eating disorders or illegal activity. App stores and device operating systems would also have to verify ages, link minors to a parent or guardian, and require parental approval for downloads and purchases. Uthmeier said parents deserve real control and that companies must design for safety rather than addiction.

He argued that if platforms invite Florida's children onto their services, they have a duty to keep them safe. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd praised the proposal and said stronger enforcement is needed to keep large social media and gaming companies from exploiting children. Under the bill, the Attorney General's Office would gain enforcement authority, with penalties of up to $50,000 per violation for companies that knowingly or recklessly break the rules. The proposal would also require human review of child sexual exploitation reports within 48 hours and a one-strike policy for adult offenders.

stories.Headline: AI Agents Are Here. Are Leaders Ready?
stories.Summary:
AI agents, which are computer programs that can carry out complex tasks with little or no human supervision, are drawing attention from business leaders because they could change fields such as medicine and law that have long resisted automation. Harry Kraemer, a clinical professor at Kellogg, and his collaborators Mitch Kentor, Daven Morrison, and Matt Pipke are publishing a series of articles on the business, cultural, and psychological effects of this technology, arguing that its impact could match or exceed the Industrial Revolution and unfold much faster. Their first installment, dated October 22, 2026, urges leaders to educate themselves now. Kraemer says leaders are asking how to use AI without losing their values and how to keep control of it rather than letting it control them.

The authors say leaders should look past using agents only to cut costs and consider what new work the technology makes possible. They note that past technologies, from the cotton mill to the personal computer, tended to shift work rather than eliminate it, and that new jobs often emerged. Healthcare is a clear example, since tasks like scheduling appointments, following up with patients, and renewing prescriptions can be done at very large volume, but errors in such high-stakes work carry greater risk. Kentor recommends a "human in the lead" approach in which domain experts supervise agents and verify their outputs rather than doing the work themselves. The authors also warn that removing entry-level roles could turn the organizational pyramid into a diamond, weakening the pipeline of future senior leaders, so companies will need new training routes for junior staff.

Kraemer, Kentor, Morrison, and Pipke present these views as their own analysis, and Kraemer in particular stresses that values depend on trust, heart, and care, which he does not believe AI will change. Morrison argues that emotions are useful data for solving problems and keep leaders in touch with reality. Pipke predicts that agents could make it easier for talented workers to leave and start small firms, which would make retention and company culture more important. The article frames the coming years as a time for leaders to build understanding and judgment before deciding how these tools are deployed. Kraemer suggests that time saved by automation could let leaders focus on developing people and building trust.

Articles.Title: AI Agents Are Here. Are Leaders Ready?
AI agents are ready to shop. Some retailers are wary.

stories.Headline: Dext launches AI Connector for accounting practices
stories.Summary:
Dext, the bookkeeping automation platform owned by IRIS Software Group, has launched AI Connector, a feature that lets accounting and bookkeeping practices query their own Dext data through Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot. The announcement came on October 22 and 23, 2026, and the feature is available at no extra cost to Dext Advanced partners in the UK, Canada, the US, Australia and New Zealand. Dext says the tool lets staff ask questions in plain language about client cash positions, health scores, workflow bottlenecks, compliance issues, data health and team performance. The company presents it as a response to the growing use of general-purpose AI tools in accounting work, which often lack the financial context of a particular practice.

Partners connect the service once through their Dext account, after which AI Connector is listed in the Claude directory, works as a ChatGPT plugin and is compatible with Copilot. Once linked, the chosen AI system retrieves only the specific data needed to answer a query, and the response is then handled by that provider, whether OpenAI, Anthropic or Microsoft. Access is read-only and limited to what a user already has permission to see in Dext, so the tool cannot alter records. Examples given include identifying clients with the lowest health scores or those missing a dividends account before year-end.

Dext's chief executive, Sabby Gill, said general-purpose AI does not know a practice's real figures, and that AI Connector puts the same Dext data users already rely on into the AI tools they already use. He described the launch as an early step that the company expects to build on. Stephen Edginton, the company's chief product and technology officer, said the feature is designed to retrieve information rather than make decisions, so that practices keep every professional judgement. Dext also advised firms to review the data policies of whichever AI provider they select, since that provider's own rules apply to each exchange.

The launch sits within a broader trend of accounting firms using consumer and workplace AI tools in daily work, which Dext says has created risks when chatbot answers do not reflect a client's actual books. The company notes that its AI products are built on a base of more than 2 billion receipts and invoices collected over 16 years. Dext is used by more than 12,000 accounting and bookkeeping firms and 700,000 businesses worldwide, and processes more than 350 million documents each year. The company has said it will keep investing in this area, though the articles do not give a timetable for further features.
